research.headline: 200 Hubspace bulbs in one 34x37 ft room is solvable with 4-6 low-power APs at ~35-50 clients per 2.4GHz radio on a WPA2-only/20MHz/channels-1-6-11 network — the real bottlenecks are Hubspace's strictly one-bulb-at-a-time app+QR provisioning (no bulk claiming, ~7-17 labor-hours for 200 units) and Afero cloud rate limits, not raw Wi-Fi capacity.

findings.claim: Hubspace A19 bulbs are 2.4GHz-only Wi-Fi (802.11 b/g/n class) with Bluetooth LE required for setup — confirmed by the official EcoSmart use-and-care guide
findings.detail: The official manual for the A19 RGBW bulb (model 12A19060WRGBWH1, Item 1008 588 501, FCC ID 2AB2Q-12A800STQT) states 'This Hubspace bulb requires a 2.4GHz Wi-Fi network' and 'the Hubspace app will only show Wi-Fi networks compatible with this bulb' (it filters out 5GHz SSIDs), and 'Bluetooth access is required for product setup' with the phone within BLE range of the bulb. The manual carries Wi-Fi CERTIFIED and Bluetooth logos. No 5GHz support of any kind.

findings.claim: There is NO bulk/batch provisioning: every Hubspace bulb must be added individually in the mobile app, with QR-code scan as the fastest path; each QR is unique to one device and doubles as a typeable numeric code
findings.detail: Official manual: 'Each smart Hubspace bulb must be added individually by scanning the QR code or by following the instructions for manual set up... Scanning the QR code is the fastest method... QR code must be scanned from inside the Hubspace app.' The QR is printed on the bulb housing AND on the boxed Quick Start Guide card; 'The QR code are numbers. You can enter those in manually instead of scanning'; 'Can I scan the same QR code to add multiple products? No. Each product has a unique QR code.' If no QR is available, a manual flow (power on bulb, tap +, Search button) discovers it over BLE. Plan physical logistics: keep each bulb's quick-start card or photograph the bulb-neck QR before installing bulbs 10 ft up in the canopy grid — scanning QRs on installed overhead bulbs will be miserable.

findings.claim: Moving a device between Hubspace accounts is a documented QR-based re-claim: scanning the QR from the new account 'will transfer it to your account' — no factory reset required
findings.detail: The A19 manual troubleshooting table answers 'A product is on another account. How do I transfer it?' with 'Scan the QR code and it will transfer to your account.' This is the sanctioned mechanism for redistributing the 200 canopy bulbs plus vignette devices across the separate per-vignette accounts Home Depot recommends, and for post-show asset handling. Untested at scale and unclear whether Wi-Fi credentials survive the transfer (bench-verify); also implies physical QR possession equals ownership, so guard the quick-start cards.

findings.claim: No official factory-reset procedure is published in the A19 manual; the community-standard reset for Hubspace bulbs is a rapid power on/off cycle (3-5 flicks) until the bulb flashes
findings.detail: The official manual's troubleshooting only offers Bluetooth off/on, phone restart, and re-scan — no reset sequence. Third-party guidance for Hubspace bulbs describes flicking the switch on/off 3-5 times until the bulb blinks to reset, and the generic smart-bulb pattern (on 10s, then 5x off/on 2s cycles until flash) applies to most Wi-Fi bulbs. Treat the exact sequence as unverified until bench-tested on the production SKU; also note that in a 40-bulb zone on one breaker, a power-cycle 'reset' pattern could accidentally reset an entire zone — resets should be done per-socket, another argument for per-zone switched circuits with individual lamp control during commissioning.

findings.claim: The community control stack (aioafero) is control-only — it CANNOT provision/claim devices; onboarding is app-exclusive, and aioafero now supports Afero's 'Conclave' push channel for near-real-time state
findings.detail: aioafero docs describe auth (AferoBridgeV1, refresh tokens), 13 typed device controllers (lights, locks, fans, switches, thermostats, security, etc.) and a 'Conclave push channel' for real-time updates, but no add-device/claiming API — the Hubspace phone app with BLE is the only claiming path. The jdeath Home Assistant integration README confirms: 'Conclave push updates are enabled by default for near real-time device changes. REST polling remains as a true-up (default every 15 minutes / 900 seconds).' This matters for the kiosk bridge: subscribe to Conclave for state, send commands via REST, and do NOT design any provisioning automation around aioafero.

findings.claim: Afero cloud rate-limits aggressively: a maintained Hubspace HA integration floors device-state refresh at 2 seconds and splits cheap delta polls from expensive full-discovery calls (hourly) specifically because of Afero throttling
findings.detail: The Emkraan/homeassistant-hubspace README documents state polling default 30s with a hard floor: 'Floored at 2s - Afero rate-limits aggressively', device discovery (full metadata) default 3600s, and notes Hubspace is 'cloud_polling — there is no local control path.' A jdeath PR (#262) split polling from discovery 'to reduce bandwidth by up to 91%'. For 5 zones x 40 bulbs, this argues for group-level commands, Conclave push instead of tight polling, and possibly sharding the canopy across accounts if per-account limits bite — no public numeric rate-limit (req/min) is documented anywhere.

findings.claim: Afero's architecture makes the phone app a literal hub: devices normally speak Wi-Fi direct to Afero Cloud, but the app can proxy control over BLE when Wi-Fi is absent — meaning 200 installed bulbs are also 200 live BLE radios in the room
findings.detail: Afero developer docs: the mobile app 'functions as a hub, securely sending and receiving messages to and from the Afero Cloud on behalf of the smart device' over BLE; hubs connect to cloud 'via Wi-Fi or LTE'. The A19 manual confirms: a product in a no-Wi-Fi location can be used via 'the app on a phone with an internet connection like LTE. The phone must be within Bluetooth range.' Implications: (1) a staff phone with cellular can rescue/control individual bulbs if the venue Wi-Fi dies, one at a time; (2) BLE advertising from ~200 bulbs adds a small 2.4GHz noise floor (BLE ads are microseconds-long on 3 advertising channels that sit between Wi-Fi 1/6/11 — low real impact, worth a spectrum scan at bench).

findings.claim: Hubspace hardware is built by Leedarson (FCC grantee 2AB2Q = Leedarson Lighting Co., Zhangzhou China); a torn-down Hubspace dimmer used an ESP32-based Leedarson LA02301 module with write-protected flash — ESP32-class silicon explains the 2.4GHz-only + BLE combo and WPA2 expectations
findings.detail: The A19 bulb's FCC ID 2AB2Q-12A800STQT resolves to Leedarson Lighting's grantee code (fccid.io/2AB2Q lists their applications; fccid.io/fcc.report block automated fetching so internal photos were not retrievable). An elektroda.com teardown of the Hubspace 500W dimmer identified an ESP32 with the Leedarson LA02301 module, flash write-protected (no OpenBeken/Tasmota path). ESP32 family = 802.11 b/g/n 2.4GHz 20MHz + BLE, WPA2-PSK universally solid, WPA3/PMF support only in newer SDK builds and frequently absent in vendor firmware. Extrapolation from dimmer to bulb is plausible (same ODM) but unconfirmed for the A19 SKU.

findings.claim: Run the bulb network as WPA2-PSK (AES/CCMP) ONLY with PMF disabled; WPA3-only breaks IoT outright and even WPA2/WPA3 transition mode (which forces PMF-capable behavior) causes join failures on legacy clients
findings.detail: Evan McCann's UniFi guide: WPA2 'more universally supported', PMF 'leave disabled for WPA2 networks'; multiple sources document that WPA3-only or mixed WPA2/WPA3 mode causes smart bulbs to fail at the 'connecting to Wi-Fi' stage, and the standard fix for Hubspace-class gear is a dedicated 2.4GHz WPA2-PSK(AES) SSID. No official Hubspace WPA3 statement exists — the manual is silent on security mode — so WPA2-only is the safe engineering default, with a 5-bulb WPA2/WPA3-transition join test as an optional bench item. Also keep SSID/PSK to plain alphanumerics (8-63 printable ASCII) and do NOT use a hidden SSID: special characters and hidden SSIDs are recurring smart-bulb join killers.

findings.claim: Design anchor for AP count: Cisco's high-density guidance is ~25 clients per radio (50 per dual-band AP) for good QoE, with real-world 50-60 clients/radio sustained at Mobile World Congress and 100/radio only with bandwidth shaping — so 200 bulbs wants 4-6 APs with 2.4GHz enabled, ~35-50 bulbs per radio
findings.detail: Cisco Wireless High Client Density Design Guide and Meraki guidance: plan ~25 clients/radio for QoE; GSMA MWC (1200+ APs) ran 50-60 clients per radio; densest deployments shape to 4-8 Mbps/client to hit 100/radio. Hubspace bulbs are near-zero-throughput clients (tiny MQTT/TLS keepalives + occasional commands), so the binding constraint is association/management overhead, not bandwidth — 40-50 bulbs/radio is comfortably inside proven territory. With only 3 non-overlapping 2.4GHz channels (1/6/11 at 20MHz), the ceiling in ONE room is effectively 3-6 co-located radios: recommend 5-6 APs (two APs may share a channel at opposite corners at minimum TX power), giving 33-40 bulbs per AP plus headroom for the ~10-20 staff/kiosk/vignette clients.

findings.claim: Hard association ceilings are far above the design point: Meraki documents 256 clients/radio (Wi-Fi 5 Wave 2) and 512 clients/radio (Wi-Fi 6) as theoretical maxima; Ruckus R550 claims 512 clients/AP with BeamFlex+; UniFi U6 marketing claims 300+ clients/AP — none of these are design targets
findings.detail: Meraki: 'Wi-Fi 5 Wave 2: 256 clients per radio... Wi-Fi 6: 512 clients per radio = 1024 per AP' explicitly labeled theoretical and 'not something we want to design for.' Ruckus R550 datasheet: 'Up to 512 clients per AP', 2.4GHz radio 2x2:2 up to 574 Mbps, BeamFlex+ 64 antenna patterns per band (Ruckus's polarization-diversity antennas have the best reputation for misbehaving cheap IoT clients). UniFi U6 line: '300+ client' claims (U6-Pro '350+'). Practical takeaway: a single premium AP could technically associate all 200 bulbs, but airtime contention, DHCP/TLS reconnect storms, and single-point-of-failure risk make 4-6 mid-tier APs (U6-Pro/U6+, Omada EAP670, or Ruckus R550/R650 class) the right architecture; UniFi is the budget-sane choice, Ruckus the premium de-risk choice.

findings.claim: Beacon/management airtime is controllable to low single digits: at a 6 Mbps basic rate, 2 SSIDs on one AP measured ~1.1% channel utilization and 10 SSIDs ~5.6-8%, but at a 1 Mbps basic rate 11 SSIDs project to ~70% — so run ONE SSID, 20MHz, and raise the minimum basic rate after bench-validating the bulbs
findings.detail: wifi-professionals.com validated the Revolution Wi-Fi SSID Overhead Calculator against live capture: 2 SSIDs/1 AP @6Mbps = 1.12% predicted vs ~1% measured; 10 SSIDs = 5.62% predicted vs ~8% measured; 14 SSIDs/2 co-channel APs = ~11%; legacy 1 Mbps beacon rate with 11 SSIDs on a shared channel ≈ 70% utilization before any data flows. Design rule for the canopy VLAN: exactly 1 SSID on the 2.4GHz radios, disable 802.11b rates (set minimum/basic rate to 6, 11 or 12 Mbps — McCann notes 'disabling rates below 6 or 11 Mbps can improve efficiency of higher-density networks' but must be compatibility-tested against the bulbs), beacon interval left at 100ms, and disable extra SSIDs on those radios (each UniFi AP supports 4-8 SSIDs/band — use as few as possible). Keep guest/kiosk/staff SSIDs on 5GHz radios only.

findings.claim: UniFi-specific IoT settings consensus: 20MHz width on 2.4GHz, channels 1/6/11 only, LOWERED transmit power (high TX power hurts in dense co-channel rooms), band steering off for IoT SSIDs, multicast/broadcast control enabled, and optionally pin groups of bulbs to specific APs via AP groups
findings.detail: HostiFi's UniFi IoT guide: use non-overlapping 1/6/11, 'lower transmit power on 2.4GHz access points', create IoT SSIDs scoped to single APs via AP groups because cheap IoT clients 'were never designed to deal with one SSID being broadcast multiple times from different APs' (they associate to a random/weak AP and never roam). For the static canopy this AP-pinning trick maps perfectly onto the 5-zone structure: e.g. 5 SSID-to-AP-group mappings (one per zone of 40 bulbs, matching the 5 separate accounts) guarantees even client distribution instead of 120 bulbs dogpiling one AP — at the cost of 5 SSIDs total, still fine at 6-12Mbps beacon rates if each radio carries only its own zone's SSID. McCann adds: enable Multicast and Broadcast Control (filters chatty broadcast) for high-density, leave DTIM auto, WPA2 + PMF off.

findings.claim: DHCP is trivial at this scale if sized deliberately: use a /23 or larger flat scope (510+ hosts) on the IoT VLAN, alert at 80% utilization, and plan for the reconnect burst — the risky moment is 200 bulbs DHCP-ing and re-establishing TLS simultaneously after a power cut, which the 5-zone circuit design should stagger
findings.detail: High-density event guidance: /24 (254 hosts) is the classic failure ('can exceed the limit within minutes'), convert dense VLANs to /22 (1022) or /21 (2046); keep pools under 80% at peak; short 1-4h leases suit churny guest networks but for ~230 static devices a 12-24h lease with a /23 avoids both exhaustion and renewal chatter. Reserve static DHCP mappings for kiosk, bridge, APs, and vignette iPads. Operationally: bring canopy zones up one 40-bulb circuit at a time (30-60s apart) at doors-open to avoid a 200-client association+DHCP+TLS thundering herd on the APs and the Afero cloud connection.

findings.claim: Bulbs permanently store the provisioned SSID+password and there is no remote credential update: changing the network name or PSK after provisioning orphans every bulb until each is individually re-onboarded — freeze SSID/PSK before the first of 200 bulbs is claimed
findings.detail: Hubspace support traffic confirms devices lose connection permanently when the router/SSID/password changes ('the transformer is still linked to your old WiFi... stored network credentials no longer match') and the fix is per-device re-setup through the app. For the activation: finalize network naming, PSK, and security mode in the shop BEFORE provisioning begins, provision against the exact production SSID (bring the actual event APs to the provisioning bench), and never touch credentials after install. A same-SSID/same-PSK spare AP is also the correct hot-spare strategy — bulbs will rejoin any AP broadcasting the identical WPA2 SSID.

findings.claim: Cellular WAN redundancy: Peplink MAX BR1 Pro 5G (~$700-900 street, one listing $1,233.99) provides hot-failover/WAN-smoothing between wired venue internet and 5G; the cheaper pattern is a Balance 20X (~$500) with cellular FlexModule or a 5G business-internet gateway as secondary WAN
findings.detail: Since ALL control (kiosk bridge -> Afero cloud -> bulbs) and even the Hubspace app die without internet, dual-WAN is mandatory for the show. Peplink MAX BR1 Pro 5G: 5G/LTE Cat-20, Wi-Fi 6, hot failover + WAN smoothing, InControl2 cloud management, proven in event/mobile deployments; Balance 20X supports xDSL primary + up to two cellular links via FlexModule Mini. Cradlepoint (E-series + NetCloud) is the enterprise alternative with strong IoT protocol support. Note two latency caveats for acceptance targets: cellular adds ~30-80ms (irrelevant vs the <2s scene-start target), and carrier CGNAT is fine because all Afero connections are outbound TLS. Order SIMs early and verify 5G band coverage inside the Charleston venue during the site survey; a dual-SIM (Verizon+T-Mobile) config covers carrier-level outages.

findings.claim: No public per-account device cap exists for Hubspace/Afero, and no documented real-world installation approaches 200 devices on one account — the largest visible community installs are a few dozen devices, making the 200-bulb single-account (or even 5x40) configuration genuinely unproven territory
findings.detail: Neither the Home Depot Hubspace FAQ, the app-store listings, the A19 manual, nor the HA integration repos state any device limit per account; GitHub issue mining on jdeath/Hubspace-Homeassistant surfaced no 'I have 100+ devices' reports; HA community threads describe the integration as workable but 'updates are slow and the UI can be unresponsive' even at hobbyist scale. Home Depot's own advice to the project (separate accounts per vignette) is consistent with known cloud-side throttling rather than an association limit. The 5-accounts-for-5-zones split (40 bulbs each) both shards any per-account rate limit and matches the aioafero one-account-per-bridge-instance model — but the Sep 23 bench gate should include the largest single-account bulb count you can assemble.

findings.claim: Provisioning labor estimate: at the app's one-at-a-time cadence (~2-5 min per bulb including QR scan, BLE handshake, Wi-Fi join, cloud registration, naming, and room/group assignment), 200 bulbs cost roughly 7-17 person-hours — parallelize with one phone per account/zone since a single account's app session is the serialization point
findings.detail: Home Depot marketing claims setup 'in less than 5 minutes' per product and reviewers corroborate a few minutes per device when nothing goes wrong; failures (QR won't scan -> toggle Bluetooth, retry; wrong network cached) add retries. Five zones x five phones x 40 bulbs at ~3 min average is about 2 hours of parallel wall-clock work — schedule provisioning as a dedicated pre-install bench day (label each bulb with zone+grid position while its QR card is in hand), NOT during the Oct 20-23 install window. Unknown and bench-critical: whether Afero's cloud rate-limits rapid sequential claims on one account (e.g., bulb #35 starts failing), and whether two phones on the SAME account can claim concurrently.

findings.claim: Wi-Fi 7 / newest-gen APs buy nothing for this project: 2.4GHz-only b/g/n clients get zero benefit from U7/6E/7 features, and 6GHz-capable APs sometimes complicate 2.4GHz IoT onboarding (WPA3 requirements on merged SSIDs)
findings.detail: The bulbs are legacy 20MHz b/g/n clients; per-AP 2.4GHz radios remain 2x2 or 4x4 across U6/U7/Ruckus generations, so capacity per radio is essentially unchanged — spend budget on MORE mid-tier APs and clean channel reuse rather than flagship models. 6GHz-inclusive SSIDs mandate WPA3-SAE which, when carelessly merged with 2.4GHz on one SSID name, silently enables transition mode and breaks IoT joins — a recurring failure mode in mixed fleets. A dedicated 2.4GHz-only WPA2 SSID sidesteps the whole class of problems.

bench_tests: Association-density knee test: join 60-70 bulbs to ONE AP's 2.4GHz radio (production AP model, 20MHz, WPA2-only, channel 6), then run 100 scene changes; record channel utilization, join stability, and scene-apply latency distribution to find the practical per-radio ceiling before finalizing AP count (target: confirm 40-50/radio is comfortable).

Minimum-basic-rate compatibility: on the test SSID, disable 802.11b rates (min/basic = 12 Mbps), power-cycle 10 bulbs and confirm they rejoin and pass traffic; repeat at 6 Mbps and at default-all-rates. If bulbs fail at 12, fall back to 6; if they fail at 6, document that 1-2 Mbps beacons are required and re-run the density test.

Security-mode join matrix: 5 bulbs x {WPA2-PSK/PMF-off, WPA2-PSK/PMF-optional, WPA2/WPA3-transition, WPA3-only} — record join success and time-to-join for each; expected result is WPA2/PMF-off works and WPA3-only fails, validating the network spec.

Provisioning-at-scale drill: time 10 consecutive QR onboardings on one account/one phone (capture per-bulb minutes and any cloud errors after N rapid claims); then attempt simultaneous claiming from TWO phones logged into the SAME account; then claim bulb #11 from a different account by scanning its QR to verify the documented cross-account transfer works while the bulb is online, and note whether Wi-Fi credentials survive the transfer.

Power-cut recovery storm: with 40 provisioned bulbs on one AP, kill mains for 10 minutes, restore all at once, and measure time until 100% report online/controllable (DHCP burst + TLS reconnect); repeat restoring in two 20-bulb waves 30s apart to quantify the benefit of staggered zone power-up against the <60s recovery acceptance target.

Credential-freeze validation: change ONLY the Wi-Fi password on the test AP and confirm 3 bulbs become permanently unreachable (no remote credential update) and require full app re-onboarding — proves the 'lock SSID/PSK before provisioning' rule to the whole team.

Factory-reset procedure discovery: on 3 production A19 bulbs, test the community reset (rapid on/off x3, x5, and 10s-on/2s-cycles variants) and document the exact sequence and blink signature that returns a bulb to pairing mode, since the official manual omits it.

5G failover cutover: run the kiosk bridge through a Peplink (or equivalent) with venue WAN primary + 5G secondary; yank the primary WAN mid-scene-change and measure (a) time until Afero commands succeed again, (b) whether Conclave push reconnects automatically, and (c) scene-apply latency over cellular vs wired — validates the <10s worst-case scene target under failover.

BLE + Wi-Fi coexistence floor: with all ~200 bulbs powered in the shop, capture a 2.4GHz spectrum scan (e.g., WiFiman/Chanalyzer) and confirm BLE advertising from the fleet does not raise noise floor materially on channels 1/6/11; simultaneously verify the Hubspace app can still BLE-control one bulb from 10 ft away through the RF crowd.

AP-pinning distribution test: configure 5 SSIDs (one per zone) each broadcast by only its zone's AP via AP groups, verify each provisioned zone's 40 bulbs associate only to their AP and the client-count spread stays 40/40/40/40/40 after a full power cycle (guards against the sticky-random-association failure mode of one shared SSID).
open_questions: Is there any hard or soft per-account device cap on Hubspace/Afero accounts, and do rapid sequential claims (40+ bulbs in an hour) trip cloud-side anti-abuse throttling? No public documentation; only the Sep 23 bench can answer.

What are the actual numeric Afero cloud API rate limits (requests/min per account, per token, per IP) and does the kiosk's 5-zone fan-out (5 accounts from one venue IP) share any per-IP bucket? Community code only reveals a 2s practical floor.

Does the QR-based cross-account transfer preserve the bulb's stored Wi-Fi credentials (pure cloud re-claim) or force a full BLE re-provision — and does it work while the bulb is online on the old account?

Exact Wi-Fi silicon in the current-production A19 RGBW bulb (ESP32-class Leedarson module like the dimmer's LA02301, or Realtek): fccid.io/fcc.report block automated retrieval of the 2AB2Q-12A800STQT internal photos — pull them manually or tear down one bulb, since chipset determines min-rate and PMF tolerance.
Do Hubspace bulbs tolerate an 802.11b-disabled network (basic rate 6-12 Mbps)? No public reports either way; this single setting is worth ~3-10x beacon-airtime savings and must be bench-proven.

Will 5 co-located 2.4GHz radios at minimum TX power in a 34x37 ft room (two channel pairs reused) stay below ~50% channel utilization during a full 200-bulb scene cascade? Needs the density bench plus a utilization capture; if not, fall back to 3 APs / ~67 bulbs each (still under Meraki Wave-2 limits but past Cisco's comfort number).
Venue RF environment in the Charleston space: neighboring-tenant 2.4GHz networks, and in-venue 5G carrier coverage for the failover SIM (site survey item, unanswerable remotely).

research.headline: The Hubspace control path is cloud-only REST on Google Cloud with per-account quotas, an undocumented rate limit (community floor: 2s polling), a default of only 3 concurrent connections per host in aioafero, and a new subscribe-only Conclave push channel — meaning 200-bulb scene fan-out speed is entirely unproven publicly and must be bench-measured, while state feedback is now near-real-time.

findings.claim: Commands cannot be batched or pushed: the June-2026 Conclave push channel is subscribe-only, so every bulb state change is an individual REST call
findings.detail: aioafero's official docs state verbatim: 'Conclave is subscribe-only. Writes still go through controller methods / bridge.send_service_request (REST).' Conclave (added in aioafero PR #77, merged 2026-06-08) is a raw TLS socket (not websocket) to conclave-stream1.afero.net:443 delivering attr_change/status_change/invalidate events that patch the same cached device models REST polling uses. For the Color Canopy this means a 5-zone scene change = up to 200 individual PUTs to /v1/accounts/{id}/metadevices/{deviceId}/state; Conclave only gives you fast per-bulb confirmation feedback for the kiosk UI, not fast application.

findings.claim: Afero rate-limits aggressively but no public numeric threshold exists anywhere; the only observed bounds are a 2s polling floor and degradation seen at 10s polling
findings.detail: The Emkraan/homeassistant-hubspace README (from-scratch 2026 integration) says: 'State polling interval | 30s | ... Floored at 2s - Afero rate-limits aggressively.' aioafero's official troubleshooting doc: 'The API rate-limits requests. Concurrent clients (phone app, Home Assistant, scripts) compete for the same quota. Reduce polling frequency with polling_interval or limit concurrent integrations.' Real-world: HA user llealloo (2025-07-18) changed polling 30s->10s and subsequently lost device names in API responses ('so maybe I got API rate limited?'); aioafero maintainer Expl0dingBanana replied (2025-07-20) 'It could be due to rate limiting.' Notably rate limiting manifested as degraded/partial responses, not clean 429s. No GitHub issue in jdeath/Hubspace-Homeassistant, aioafero, or Emkraan repos documents an actual 429 threshold, requests/min number, or IP ban.

findings.claim: aioafero handles 429/503/504 as silently retryable with tiny linear backoff and caps concurrency at 3 connections per host — a built-in throughput ceiling you must patch for 200 bulbs
findings.detail: In src/aioafero/v1/__init__.py: 'if resp.status in [429, 503, 504]: continue' inside 'while retries < v1_const.MAX_RETRIES' (MAX_RETRIES=3) with retry_wait = 0.25 * retries (0.25s/0.5s/0.75s); 403s are tracked separately and after STATE_FETCH_FORBIDDEN_LIMIT=3 consecutive 403s a device's state polling is paused until rediscovery. The aiohttp session is created with TCPConnector(limit_per_host=3). At 3 concurrent in-flight requests, 200 PUTs at an optimistic ~200-300ms RTT each ≈ 13-20s first-to-last spread — would fail the <2s spread target. The kiosk bridge must raise limit_per_host and/or split accounts; whether Afero's server side tolerates that is the key bench unknown.

findings.claim: Observed single-command latency on the cloud path is roughly 1-2 seconds app-to-bulb when healthy; 'almost instant' state feedback is reported with current integrations
findings.detail: GitHub issue #34 (jdeath repo, 2023-04-14): 'The delay on sending the request is 1 to 2 sec and that is fine but if I want to do automation...it is taking 120 sec to run' (the 120s was the old poll-based architecture, since fixed). Hubspace support in Home Depot product Q&A: on Wi-Fi control 'should be pretty much instantly responsive,' on Bluetooth 'a couple of seconds.' HA user OvalZyre (2025-01-30): devices 'have been stellar for months - showing status almost instantly in HASS.' Worst path: Reviewed.com's review measured Alexa voice->Hubspace at 15-20s ('Alexa pauses to think about what I'm asking for 15 to 20 seconds') — avoid third-party voice chains at the activation. No one has published p95 command RTT measurements; the <2s visible-start target is plausible but unproven at fan-out scale.

findings.claim: Access tokens live only 118 seconds; aioafero refreshes proactively with a 2s buffer — expect a token refresh roughly every 2 minutes per account, times 5-9 accounts
findings.detail: aioafero auth.py: DEFAULT_TOKEN_TIMEOUT = 118, TOKEN_EXPIRY_BUFFER = 2, expiration = timestamp + expires_in - buffer. Auth is OAuth2 code+PKCE against Keycloak at accounts.hubspaceconnect.com. Conclave access tokens are separate, short-lived and effectively single-use: docs say always mint a fresh one via POST /v1/accounts/{accountId}/conclaveAccess on every reconnect and do not trust expires_timestamp. This is background load to account for in the soak test but not a latency problem per se.

findings.claim: Multiple accounts in parallel has a documented rationale (quota is per-account/shared across clients) but zero public proof as a throughput multiplier; per-IP throttling is unknown
findings.detail: aioafero's troubleshooting doc says concurrent clients 'compete for the same quota,' implying quota is keyed to the account — so 5 zone-accounts should have 5 independent quotas, matching Home Depot's own advice of separate accounts per vignette. Hubspace's account model supports this cleanly: devices live in 'Homes' under one account and 'You cannot share devices among Homes'; sharing = sharing credentials. But no GitHub issue, forum post, or doc demonstrates aggregate throughput scaling with account count, and nothing public says whether Afero also throttles per source IP (all kiosk accounts would share one NAT IP at the venue). No public IP-ban reports found at all.

findings.claim: Conclave push mechanics: ~60s server heartbeats, ~120s staleness detection, 60s login deadline, 1s->60s exponential reconnect backoff — no published push latency figures
findings.detail: From aioafero conclave/client.py and docs: server advertises heartbeat in hello/welcome ('typically ~60 seconds', sent as bare \n); DEFAULT_READ_TIMEOUT=75.0s with wire-idle multiplier 2.0 (~120s staleness); DEFAULT_INITIAL_BACKOFF=1.0s doubling to DEFAULT_MAX_BACKOFF=60.0s; login must complete within 60s or 'push updates may be delayed'; READ_CHUNK_SIZE=65536; optional zlib compression; optional push_idle_timeout catches zombie sessions (ConclavePushStaleError). Events (attr_change/status_change) flow straight into device cache with no debounce/coalescing constants. Nobody has published tap-to-push-event latency; jdeath README calls it 'near real-time device changes'. For recovery: fresh conclaveAccess token per reconnect + max 60s backoff means the <60s internet-recovery target is architecturally reachable but needs verification.

findings.claim: REST polling is heavyweight: 14 lights polled at 5s consumed ~1.5 GB/day (~87 KB per poll cycle); 200 bulbs would multiply this — size the venue uplink and prefer Conclave
findings.detail: GitHub issue #216 (jdeath repo, 2025-12-30): 'my Hubspace integration has been using gigabytes of data per day. I dropped my polling rate from 5 to 30 seconds and it reduced it by a factor of 5' — ~1.5GB/day with 14 lights, measured over 30 minutes via HA System Monitor. Scaling naively, 200 bulbs at 30s polling could be on the order of 4+ GB/day of API traffic; Conclave push plus a slow REST true-up (jdeath v8 default: 900s) is the current-generation answer. jdeath v8.3.0 enables Conclave by default with 'REST polling remains as a true-up (default every 15 minutes / 900 seconds)'.

findings.claim: Afero cloud runs on Google Cloud (not AWS), has no public status page and no DownDetector/IsTheServiceDown coverage; outage signal exists only as anecdotes, including a >=43-minute 500-error event in July 2026
findings.detail: DNS resolved today: api2.afero.net = 35.184.28.9 (PTR *.bc.googleusercontent.com), accounts.hubspaceconnect.com = same IP, semantics2.afero.net = 34.49.181.0 (GCP LB range), conclave-stream1.afero.net = 34.10.95.66 — all Google Cloud, so the famous 2025-10-20 AWS us-east-1 14h outage would not have hit Afero's API directly (it did kill Alexa/Ring paths; note your install week is that outage's anniversary, and GCP had its own major outage 2025-06-12). istheservicedown.com/problems/hubspace returns 404; no status.afero.io found. Documented incidents: GitHub issue #240 (2026-07-27) logged 500 Internal Server Error + connection timeouts to api2.afero.net for at least 43 minutes (10:07-10:50 AM); HA thread user jaaem (2025-01-31): 'Sometimes the API gets overloaded'; JustUseApp complaint tracker shows a constant stream (70 reports/24h; 27.0% connection issues, 19.8% not working, 11.7% login; complaints like 'app takes at least 5 minutes to load', 'all products are offline'). Plan for cloud loss with no vendor status page to point at.

findings.claim: Library/ecosystem status September 2026: aioafero 9.3.0 (released 4 days ago) is the current, very active library; the rename chain is hubspace_async -> aiohubspace (dead at 1.2.0, Apr 2025) -> aioafero; jdeath integration is at v8.3.0; a rival Emkraan integration focuses on exactly your failure modes
findings.detail: PyPI: aioafero 9.3.0 (2026-09-15), 9.2.1 (09-13), 9.2.0 (09-12), 9.1.0 (09-03), 9.0.1 (08-09) — fast release cadence, Python >=3.12; aiohubspace last release 1.2.0 on 2025-04-07 ('updated from hubspace_async'). aioafero 8.0.0 (June 2026) decoupled auth from bridge; Conclave landed in the same window. Emkraan/homeassistant-hubspace is a separate from-scratch integration targeting 'devices that go unavailable and never recover' and 'commands that appear to work then silently revert' ('Historically the most common Hubspace complaint - a stale poll response overwriting an optimistic update'), with per-device availability, self-healing reload escalation, and a 10-min stale-data grace period to ride out 'brief Afero cloud blips' — its design choices are a checklist of the failure modes your kiosk bridge must handle.

findings.claim: Historic maintainer verdict (older jdeath README, since removed): Hubspace updates are slow and the UI unresponsive, recommending other devices for HA integration
findings.detail: Search-indexed text from the jdeath repo (older README revision, pre-v5; the sentence is absent from v5.10.0 and current v8.3.0 READMEs which only note 'Due to the cloud-first nature of Hubspace devices, an internet connection needs to be available, along with the Hubspace servers'): updates are slow, the UI can be unresponsive, devices are 100% cloud-reliant, and the developer 'would highly recommend finding another device.' The removal of this warning coincides with the aioafero rewrite + Conclave push era, suggesting the situation materially improved in 2025-2026 — but the underlying architecture (cloud round-trip per command) is unchanged.

bench_tests: Command RTT baseline: from the kiosk bridge on the venue-like network, send 100 single-bulb PUTs (one bulb, randomized colors) via aioafero 9.3.0 and measure (a) HTTP accept latency and (b) tap-to-visible-change with a phone camera at 240fps or a photodiode; report p50/p95/p99 against the <2s visible-start target.

Fan-out spread test: fire 40 concurrent PUTs (one zone) with stock TCPConnector(limit_per_host=3), then rebuild the session with limit_per_host = 10 / 20 / 40 and repeat; measure first-to-last-bulb spread each way and record any 429/503/500 responses or degraded payloads — this single test decides whether one account can meet the <2s spread target or the build needs 5 accounts.

Rate-limit threshold probe (do this on a burner account first): sustain 1, 2, 5, 10, 20 req/s of state GETs+PUTs for 10 min each; log first appearance of 429/503, response-field degradation (the community-observed 'lost device names' symptom), and cool-down time to normal service; then repeat the same ramp on two accounts simultaneously from the SAME public IP to determine whether throttling is per-account or per-IP (decides if 5 zone-accounts actually multiply throughput at the venue NAT).

Conclave feedback latency: run bridge with enable_conclave=True, send a PUT, timestamp the corresponding attr_change push arrival; 100 samples for p95 — validates using push events as the kiosk's 'scene applied' confirmation instead of polling.

8h soak at show scale: 200 bulbs across 5 accounts (5 bridge instances), scene change every 60-90s, Conclave on, REST true-up 900s; monitor per-account token refreshes (~every 116s each), Conclave reconnect counts, command queue depth, memory, and total bandwidth (compare against the ~87KB/poll figure from issue #216) — verifies zero queue growth and no cumulative throttling.

WAN-cut recovery: pull the venue uplink for 2, 10, and 30 minutes mid-show-loop; verify Conclave reconnects (fresh conclaveAccess token, backoff capped at 60s) and first successful scene change within 60s of internet restoration; also verify bulbs' own behavior (do they hold last state?) since the cloud has no offline command queue you control.

429-response autopsy: when the probe finally triggers throttling, capture exact status codes, response headers (Retry-After?), and body — no public source documents what Afero's throttle response actually looks like, and the bridge's retry logic should key off the real signal rather than aioafero's blind 0.25s-step retries.
open_questions: What is the actual numeric rate limit (requests/min) per account, and is there an additional per-IP limit? Nothing public exists — only the 2s polling floor (Emkraan) and 10s-polling degradation (July 2025 report). The 200-PUT scene burst is far outside any publicly tested envelope.

Does any server-side group/scene primitive exist in the Afero API (apply one command to N devices)? aioafero exposes only per-metadevice state PUTs; if the official app's 'groups' are client-side fan-out too, nothing saves you from 200 calls — needs MITM capture of the official app applying a group scene (aioafero docs include a MITM capture guide).

Is Afero throttling keyed to account, OAuth client, token, or source IP? Determines whether Home Depot's separate-accounts-per-vignette advice actually multiplies aggregate throughput from one kiosk NAT.
What is real Conclave push latency (ms) under load, and does it degrade during command bursts? No public measurements exist at all.
How does the largest publicly-known account (~14-50 devices) compare to 40-200 devices per account — does poll payload size or command acceptance degrade nonlinearly with device count?

Was Hubspace affected by the 2025-06-12 Google Cloud outage (relevant since DNS proves Afero is GCP-hosted, and the Oct 20 2025 AWS outage was likely a non-event for them)? Search budget ran out before confirming; worth one check.
Why did the July 2026 incident (issue #240) resolve — Afero-side fix or client fix? The issue closed without a documented root cause, so mean-time-to-recovery for Afero cloud incidents is unknown.

research.headline: There is zero public record of Afero/Home Depot ever blocking or C&D'ing the 4+year-old ecosystem of reverse-engineered Hubspace clients, but every unofficial route technically breaches a "personal, noncommercial use" license — so for a client-sanctioned commercial activation the cheap insurance is a written blessing routed through the existing THD relationship (Afero demonstrably sells commercial API access via negotiated Service Agreements), plus a zero-app-store distribution plan (PWA in Guided Access / ad-hoc signing) and nominative-fair-use discipline around the HUBSPACE mark.

findings.claim: The Hubspace app's own Terms of Use license is expressly limited to 'personal, noncommercial use' — a commercial brand activation and a replacement client both fall outside the granted license
findings.detail: The dedicated 'The Home Depot HubSpace App Terms of Use' PDF (doc #9541887, dated 6-4-2020, still served from homedepot.com) grants permission 'to view and use this App ... for your own personal, noncommercial use' and forbids modifying, distributing, or creating derivative works 'from this App'. Notably it contains NO explicit anti-bot, anti-automation, or anti-reverse-engineering clause and no unilateral account-termination clause; governing law is Georgia, venue Atlanta, and arbitration applies only 'WITH THE PRIOR AGREEMENT OF THE HOME DEPOT'. Copyright is held jointly by Home Depot Product Authority, LLC (HDPA) and Afero, Inc. Practical read: the activation is a commercial use, but the operative risk is contract/ToS breach (account termination), not any stronger hook — and the client (THD) is the counterparty who can waive it.

findings.claim: The general homedepot.com Terms of Use (updated ~June 2026) adds the prohibitions the app ToU lacks: no bots/automated access and no reverse engineering/decompiling of the Site or Content
findings.detail: Search-index text of homedepot.com/c/Terms_of_Use shows prohibitions on 'bots, crawlers, automated scripts, or other automated means' and on 'modify, adapt, translate, reverse engineer, decompile, disassemble, or create derivative works from the Site or any Content', with new 2026 AI-feature clauses. The page 403s automated fetches (Akamai), consistent with active anti-bot posture on the retail site. Whether these site terms attach to Afero-cloud API traffic from a bridge (api2.afero.net is Afero's domain, not 'the Site') is untested; the app ToU says the app terms + privacy statement 'constitute the entire agreement ... with respect to this App'. Treat as: THD claims broad anti-automation rights somewhere in the stack, so get written sanction rather than parsing which document controls.

findings.claim: Afero's Developer Terms of Service (the agreement you'd sign to get official access) bans reverse engineering, circumvention, commercialization, and even disclosing evaluation results — but ONLY binds parties who sign up; the community-library route never accepts it
findings.detail: Afero Developer ToS (last updated 12/16/2016, still live on cdn.afero.io) §3(b): without prior written approval Developer will not '(i) modify or create derivative works ... (ii) work around, interfere with, exceed or circumvent any technical limitations ... (iii) reverse engineer, decompile ... (iv) publish, rent, lease ... or otherwise commercialize ... (v) release or disclose the results of Developer's use ... to any third party other than via the Site's developer forum ... (viii) use the Afero Platform in any way that ... accesses in an unauthorized manner the servers'. §2(a): any use beyond internal evaluation 'including selling or otherwise distributing any Integrated Device' requires 'a separate commercial service agreement signed by both parties (Service Agreement)' — this is the contractual proof that Afero sells commercial platform access. §3(d): Afero may impose 'maximum use and traffic limitations' and suspend at will. §13(i) No Publicity: no press release or public announcement about a relationship with Afero without written consent — directly constrains how a 'powered by Afero/Hubspace' pitch could be marketed if you ever sign this. Choice of law: California, Santa Clara County venue. Notices to legal@afero.io.

findings.claim: Afero's API License Addendum reserves monitoring, instant revocation, and a 30-day data-retention cap — terms to expect in any blessed-access negotiation
findings.detail: Addendum A to the Developer ToS: Afero 'may change, suspend or cancel any or all of the functionality of the Afero APIs ... at any time', may suspend immediately on 'actual or reasonably suspected security breach', requires developers to update within 30 days of API revisions, treats API keys as Afero Confidential Information, and §2(c) has Developer authorize Afero 'to monitor Developer's use of the Afero APIs, including by accessing Developer Software'. Developer Data may be retained max 30 days and must be destroyed on request. If the activation negotiates sanctioned access, these are the default paper terms; a short-term event rider (fixed term Oct 15-Nov 2, named account IDs, agreed request budget) is the realistic shape.

findings.claim: Four-plus years of public, reverse-engineered Hubspace clients have operated with zero known C&Ds, DMCA takedowns, GitHub removals, or targeted blocking by Afero/Home Depot
findings.detail: jdeath/Hubspace-Homeassistant has issues dating to July 2022 (issue #6) and is still actively maintained in Sept 2026; homebridge-hubspace (sajmonr) and a from-scratch 2025+ integration (Emkraan/homeassistant-hubspace) are public with 'unofficial, not affiliated' disclaimers; the aioafero PyPI package advertises 'Talk to the Afero API asynchronously'. Targeted searches for cease-and-desist/DMCA history return nothing, and the Hubitat community thread (Feb 2025) discusses reverse-engineering openly with no enforcement anxiety. Counterpoint discipline: absence of enforcement is not permission, tolerance of hobbyist HA users is not tolerance of a branded commercial kiosk, and the one documented disruption was an apparent THD-side backend migration that made devices vanish from the API (noted in the Emkraan README), i.e., breakage risk is operational, not legal.

findings.claim: Observed anti-abuse surface is mild: aggressive request rate-limiting (community floors polling at 2s), per-device 403s under some conditions, opt-in OTP/MFA, ~2-minute access tokens — but no reports of login lockouts, CAPTCHAs, or new-device blocks
findings.detail: Emkraan README: 'State polling interval ... Floored at 2s - Afero rate-limits aggressively.' aioafero v1_const.py ships STATE_FETCH_FORBIDDEN_LIMIT=3 ('Consecutive per-device state GET 403s before pausing polls'), MAX_RETRIES=3, and DEFAULT_TOKEN_TIMEOUT=118s; jdeath README confirms a revoked session stays valid 'up to two more minutes' and that Hubspace has a 'Where You're Signed In' -> 'SIGN OUT OF ALL OTHER DEVICES' kill switch that does NOT auto-fire when MFA is enabled. aioafero implements OTPRequired/InvalidOTP flows (OTP support added Oct 2025), meaning MFA-enabled accounts challenge scripted logins — activation accounts should keep MFA off or pre-wire OTP handling. GitHub issue searches across both repos surface no 429-ban, lockout, or captcha reports; auth is standard Keycloak (realm 'thd') at accounts.hubspaceconnect.com with public OpenID discovery. Implication for the Canopy: one long-lived session per account with refresh-token reuse (aioafero's model) is the proven-quiet pattern; avoid repeated fresh password logins, which is the classic Keycloak brute-force trigger and the one thing nobody has publicly stress-tested.

findings.claim: The community client works by impersonating the official Android app — client_id 'hubspace_android' plus a spoofed Android WebView User-Agent — which is both its main fingerprinting exposure and the optics problem in any 'we did nothing sneaky' narrative
findings.detail: aioafero v1_const.py: AUTH_DEFAULT_CLIENT_ID='hubspace_android', AUTH_OPENID_HOST='accounts.hubspaceconnect.com', AUTH_REALM='thd', redirect 'hubspace-app://loginredirect', API hosts api2.afero.net and semantics2.afero.net, and DEFAULT_USERAGENT template 'Mozilla/5.0 (Linux; Android 15; ${client_name} Build/test; wv)...'. Afero can trivially distinguish real apps from bridges (TLS fingerprint, UA entropy, request cadence) whenever it chooses; it simply hasn't chosen to. For the activation this cuts two ways: (a) technical kill risk is a switch Afero already owns, so the Sep 23 bench gate should include a 'what if 403-everything' drill; (b) in a sanctioned-access pitch, proactively disclosing that today's plan-A rides the app's own OAuth client is cleaner than being discovered doing it during a co-branded event on THD property.

findings.claim: DMCA 1201/CFAA landscape (commonly cited position, not legal advice): controlling devices you own through their intended cloud API with valid credentials sits in the most defensible corner of US interoperability law
findings.detail: Chamberlain v. Skylink (Fed. Cir. 2004, 381 F.3d 1178) rejected a DMCA §1201 claim against an interoperable garage-door remote, requiring a nexus between circumvention and copyright infringement and noting buyers had implicit authorization to use interoperating products; it remains the anchor cite for third-party controllers of consumer devices. Van Buren v. United States (593 U.S. 178 (2021)) narrowed CFAA 'exceeds authorized access' to a gates-up-or-down test — using credentials you legitimately hold for a purpose the ToS dislikes is not a federal hacking crime (CRS LSB10616 summarizes). Logging into Keycloak with your own account and issuing documented REST calls circumvents no technological protection measure guarding a copyrighted work, so §1201 is largely inapposite; the residual exposure is contract (ToS breach -> account termination) and, theoretically, state-law claims. The posture worsens only if one bypasses an actual technical block (e.g., rotating credentials/IPs after a ban) — that is the line not to cross at a client activation.

findings.claim: Van Buren primary source for the CFAA half of the landscape paragraph
findings.detail: Supreme Court slip opinion, June 3 2021, holding an individual 'exceeds authorized access' only by entering parts of a system that are off-limits to them, not by misusing access they legitimately have. Companion analysis: Congressional Research Service LSB10616 (congress.gov/crs-product/LSB10616). Justia case page: supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/593/19-783/.

findings.claim: Sanctioned path exists and is concrete: Afero sells commercial platform access via negotiated Service Agreements, has a partnership intake page, and is financially intertwined with THD (Home Depot Ventures investor) — route the ask through the activation's existing THD client sponsor to the THD Hubspace merchandising team, in parallel with Afero's partnership contact
findings.detail: Afero Developer ToS §2(a)/§3(d) codify the 'separate commercial service agreement' upsell; afero.io runs a 'Contact Afero | Let's Build Something Together' intake (afero.io/html/home/contact-afero.html) and markets itself as an enterprise IoT PaaS with a Home Depot case study (afero.io/html/home/case-study-home-depot.html); Home Depot Ventures announced an investment in Afero May 2022 (afero.io/html/home/article05.10.22.html); Afero press (BusinessWire, Dec 16 2025) announced 'Hubspace 2.0' — Afero remains the operating vendor. Legal notices: legal@afero.io (from the ToS). Realistic sequencing for an Oct 20 install: (1) THD client sponsor emails an authorization letter covering ~205 activation-owned devices and named accounts ('THD authorizes vendor X to programmatically control Hubspace devices owned by THD/agency for the House Beautiful activation, Oct 15-Nov 2 2026'); (2) that sponsor introduces Afero for either a blessed rate budget on the existing consumer API or a proper API arrangement. A signed Service Agreement in 4 weeks is unlikely; the authorization letter is the achievable artifact that converts ToS breach into licensed use, since HDPA/THD is itself the counterparty of the consumer ToU. There is no public evidence Afero sells self-serve API keys or has any public 'works with Hubspace' third-party program — everything is negotiated BD.

findings.claim: Timing risk to flag in any pitch: Afero/THD shipped 'Hubspace 2.0' (Dec 2025) and a community README attributes device-vanishing incidents to a 'Home-Depot-side backend migration' — a backend change during the Oct 20-Nov 1 window is a live operational risk for an unsanctioned bridge
findings.detail: BusinessWire release 'Afero Powers the Launch of Hubspace 2.0 Smart Home Platform' (Dec 16 2025; page 403s bots but is indexed) plus the Emkraan README's per-device availability feature motivated by devices 'vanishing from Afero's API during a Home-Depot-side backend migration'. jdeath issue #240 (July 2026) shows a transient fleet-wide 500 'Internal Server Error' on device control. An unsanctioned client gets zero change notice; a sanctioned contact gets at minimum a heads-up channel. Worth stating in the go/no-go: plan-A must survive silent API-shape drift (pin aioafero version, snapshot metadevice schemas at bench time, alert on schema deltas).

findings.claim: Distribution without app-store friction is a solved problem for this activation: guest kiosk and staff iPads can run a PWA/web UI locked with Guided Access or supervised Single App Mode — zero Apple review, zero Apple program dependency
findings.detail: The bridge already implies a local web server; serving the operator/guest UI as a full-screen web app and locking Safari (or a home-screen web app) via Guided Access (Settings > Accessibility, triple-click side button, passcode-protected: support.apple.com/en-us/111795) is the lowest-friction path. For hard kiosk behavior (survives reboot, disables hardware buttons, no escape without MDM), supervise the iPads with Apple Configurator and use Single App Mode (support.apple.com/guide/apple-configurator-2/single-app-mode-features-cadb1d640325 and the Apple Platform Deployment guide's supervised-restrictions chapter). This also neatly sidesteps App Review Guideline exposure for an app that drives a reverse-engineered API — nothing is submitted to Apple at all. The 10x20 canopy kiosk itself, if it's a PC/Android touchscreen, needs no Apple pathway (Chrome --kiosk / Windows Assigned Access).

findings.claim: If a native iOS operator app is wanted anyway: ad-hoc distribution (up to 100 registered devices per device family per membership year, no review) or TestFlight internal testing are the review-free lanes; unlisted and Custom Apps still pass App Review; the $299 Enterprise Program is ineligible and inappropriate for this use
findings.detail: Apple Developer Program ($99/yr) supports ad-hoc provisioning to 100 registered UDIDs per product family per membership year (developer.apple.com/help/account/devices/devices-overview) — 4-6 activation iPads are trivially covered, profiles valid ~1 year, well past Nov 1 strike. TestFlight internal testing (up to 100 App Store Connect users) skips external Beta App Review. 'Unlisted app distribution' (link-only App Store) and Apple Business Manager Custom Apps both still undergo full App Review — friction and disclosure of the unofficial API. The Apple Developer Enterprise Program requires 100+ employees and internal-employee-only use; distributing an enterprise-signed app for a client activation is a program violation with account-ban risk (foresightmobile.com/blog/ios-app-distribution-guide-2026 summarizes current rules). Recommendation embedded in the evidence: PWA first; ad-hoc if native is forced; never enterprise certs.

findings.claim: Trademark care: HUBSPACE is a live USPTO-registered mark of Home Depot Product Authority, LLC, THD's ToU promises 'aggressive' IP enforcement and forbids using THD marks in publicity without prior written permission — so 'works with Hubspace' phrasing survives only as disciplined nominative fair use, and ideally under the activation's written brand approval instead
findings.detail: USPTO records: HUBSPACE serials 88128659 (filed 2018), 88774500, 90475268, plus HUBSPACE CONNECT serial 99163808 filed Apr 30 2025, all owned by Home Depot Product Authority, LLC (trademarks.justia.com/881/28/hubspace-88128659.html). The Hubspace App ToU states THD 'aggressively enforces its intellectual property rights' and bars use of THD names/logos 'in advertising or publicity' without prior written permission. Nominative fair use (New Kids on the Block test, codified in 9th Cir. Model Civil Jury Instructions §15.24: ce9.uscourts.gov/jury-instructions/print/book/export/html/251) permits truthful compatibility references if (1) the product isn't identifiable without the mark, (2) only as much of the mark as necessary is used (words only — never the Hubspace logo, colorway, or stylization), (3) nothing suggests sponsorship — e.g. 'Compatible with Hubspace® devices. Not affiliated with or endorsed by The Home Depot or Afero.' Inside this co-branded activation the cleaner instrument is a line item in the SOW/brand-approval chain licensing the mark for event UI; the nominative-fair-use posture matters mainly for the AFTERWARD scenario — pitching the bespoke app to other clients or publicly — where the disclaimer plus no-logo rule is mandatory and the Afero Developer ToS no-publicity clause (if ever signed) adds a consent requirement.

findings.claim: The 'bespoke replacement app' pitched commercially after the activation carries a different, heavier risk profile than the activation itself — it converts tolerated interop into a distributed commercial product built on an unlicensed API
findings.detail: Activation: THD is the client, devices/accounts are owned, use is on-site, short-lived, and effectively sanctioned — contract risk approaches zero with a sponsor letter. Productized app: distribution to third parties of a client that commercializes Afero's platform squarely conflicts with the consumer ToU ('personal, noncommercial'), would need App Review (Guideline 5.2.2/4.x exposure for unauthorized third-party service use has sunk similar unofficial clients), invites the platform-owner response that hobbyist HA integrations never provoked, and competes with Afero's own paid deliverable (they built and ship the official app — the Google Play package is literally io.afero.partner.hubspace). The defensible commercial pitch is the one aimed AT the client: a THD/Afero-licensed operator/retail experience layer, sold with their API blessing — evidenced feasible by Afero's Service Agreement structure. Pitch it as 'we'll build it on your licensed API' not 'we built it on your reverse-engineered API'.

bench_tests: Login-churn probe on a sacrificial Hubspace account: perform 5, 15, then 30 fresh password OAuth logins (PKCE flow via accounts.hubspaceconnect.com realm 'thd') within one hour from the venue IP; record at which count, if any, Keycloak returns temporary-lockout/'invalid credentials' on valid creds, an OTP challenge appears, or a security email arrives. This determines whether the 5-account architecture can survive worst-case bridge restarts during show hours.

Rate-limit ceiling measurement: with one account and ~40 real bulbs, ramp sustained request rate (state GETs + state PUTs) from 0.5 to 20 rps and log the first appearance of 429s or 403s from api2.afero.net, plus whether the throttle is per-account, per-token, or per-IP (test two accounts from one IP vs one account from two IPs). Output: a hard requests/sec budget per zone for the 200-bulb canopy.

Concurrent-session coexistence: hold the bridge's refresh-token session while logging the same account into the official Hubspace app on a staff phone; verify neither evicts the other over 24h, then trigger 'Manage Account > Where You're Signed In > SIGN OUT OF ALL OTHER DEVICES' and time bridge death (expected <=2 min) and scripted recovery — this is the documented kill switch an operator could fat-finger.

MFA/OTP posture check: confirm all 5 activation accounts have MFA disabled and that aioafero never raises OTPRequired across 50 cold re-authentications spread over 48h (including 3 AM runs); separately enable MFA on the sacrificial account to capture exactly what the OTP challenge looks like so operators recognize it.

Security-notification watch: monitor the inboxes of all activation accounts during the full soak week for 'new device sign-in' or anomaly emails triggered by the spoofed Android-WebView user agent from a datacenter-looking venue IP; zero emails = quiet fingerprint, any email = document and pre-brief client.

8-hour soak with denial telemetry: during the standard soak, log every non-200 from api2.afero.net/semantics2.afero.net by device ID and status code, specifically watching for the per-device 403 pattern aioafero's STATE_FETCH_FORBIDDEN_LIMIT was built for; any organic 403/429 during normal-rate operation changes the risk narrative and belongs in the Sep 23 go/no-go.

Ban-response fire drill: simulate a total API denial (null-route api2.afero.net at the router) mid-scene and verify the kiosk degrades gracefully (holds last scene, shows no error to guests) and that the team's plan-B decision tree (who calls whom, Art-Net fallback trigger) executes; an actual Afero-side block would look exactly like this.
open_questions: Will THD's client sponsor sign a short written authorization ('THD authorizes programmatic control of activation-owned Hubspace devices/accounts for the House Beautiful activation, Oct 15-Nov 2 2026')? This single document collapses most of the ToS-breach risk because HDPA/THD is the ToU counterparty — who on the Hearst/THD account team owns getting it?

Does Afero offer a short-term/event-scale commercial arrangement (blessed rate budget or API keys) and what is the lead time and cost? No public pricing exists; only the negotiated 'Service Agreement' path is documented — an intro through the THD Hubspace merchandising team vs cold outreach to afero.io/contact likely differ by weeks.

Do the June-2026 homedepot.com site Terms of Use legally reach Afero-cloud API traffic from a bridge, or does the app-specific 2020 ToU (no anti-automation clause, 'entire agreement' language) control? Unresolved and probably unresolvable without counsel — flag to the agency's lawyer, don't self-answer.

Is the 2020 Hubspace App ToU PDF still the version linked inside the current (Hubspace 2.0) app, or has an updated in-app ToS added anti-automation/termination clauses? Needs a 2-minute check inside the app on a bench iPad.
What are the actual Keycloak brute-force settings on realm 'thd' (lockout threshold, wait time) and is throttling per-IP or per-account? Only the bench login-churn probe answers this.

Are any backend/API changes scheduled around the Hubspace 2.0 rollout train for late Oct 2026 (the activation window)? Only answerable through a sanctioned Afero/THD contact — another argument for making that contact.

For the post-activation product pitch: would Afero/THD entertain a licensed white-label 'retail experience mode' built on their API (precedent: they already license the platform to THD itself), and does the Afero Developer ToS no-publicity clause constrain how the agency may case-study this activation? Get written case-study permission into the SOW now.
Trademark clearance for the activation UI: does the existing Hearst/THD brand-approval workflow cover on-screen use of the HUBSPACE name/logo in the kiosk UI, or is a separate HDPA sign-off needed?

research.headline: The official Hubspace app (v2.5.1, Sep 2026) is a competent consumer remote but structurally wrong for a staffed retail activation — no user-composable scenes, per-device-only schedules, multi-user via password sharing, no iPad-native UI, no demo/retail/commercial mode, and 2025-26 reviews cluster on offline-on-launch lag, login failures, and group limitations — giving a bespoke kiosk/staff app a real, evidence-backed differentiation story.

findings.claim: Current app versions and cadence: iOS 2.5.1 (released Aug 21, 2026) and Android 2.5.1 (Aug 22, 2026), with roughly monthly releases through 2026 (2.2.0 Feb 4, 2.3.0 Apr 15, 2.4.0 Jun 9, 2.5.0 Aug 18); Android changelogs are generic 'Bug fixes and Improvements'.
findings.detail: Developer is Afero, Inc. (Google Play package io.afero.partner.hubspace). The steady cadence means any bespoke app riding the same cloud must be re-verified against monthly platform updates; an app-freeze on the show iPads/kiosk during Oct 20-Nov 1 is advisable.

findings.claim: Hubspace 2.0 was a full app redesign shipped Nov 17, 2025 (iOS 2.0.0), announced by Afero Dec 16, 2025 and by Home Depot corporate Jan 7, 2026; it added Hubspace Connect (switches digitally control any Hubspace light regardless of wiring), circadian lighting, warm dimming, logarithmic dimming, and dynamic vacation mode (2.1.0, Dec 15, 2025).
findings.detail: Marketing centers on wiring-free switch-to-light binding and wellness lighting, not on scenes, groups, or multi-user. Post-redesign complaints include added navigation depth ('Now i have to enter a new sub menu...making Hubspace cumbersome when it was perfectly fine') and notification clutter ('full of notifications for things I don't want', Dec 22, 2025 review).

findings.claim: Structure: the app organizes devices by 'room and property' — multiple homes/properties per account with switching between them, and rooms within each; rooms and homes are cloud-side objects (the Afero API exposes metadevice.room and metadevice.home types).
findings.detail: A featured App Store review specifically praises switching between multiple home locations, so a single staff account could technically model the 4 vignettes as 4 'homes' — but Home Depot's advice of separate accounts per vignette remains safer for blast-radius and session reasons. Rooms give unified on/off control that one 2022 reviewer called 'extremely handy'.

findings.claim: Groups: users can create device groups (Edit Group flow to add/remove); a group of similar RGB lights exposes power, brightness, color temperature, RGB color and presets for the whole group; grouped devices remain individually controllable; NO group size limit is documented anywhere public.
findings.detail: The biggest, most persistent group complaint through late 2025 is that groups cannot hold schedules: 'Absolutely need the ability to set a schedule for GROUPED items' (Oct 27, 2025, 3 stars), 'Schedules can only be applied to individual lights...I'll have 30 schedules by the time I'm done'. Nothing in the public record shows anyone running a 40-bulb group, let alone 200 bulbs on one account — behavior at Color Canopy scale is untested territory.

findings.claim: Scenes: the app has NO user-composable multi-device scene feature (no 'capture these 40 bulbs' snapshot). What exists is per-device/group 'presets' — fixed theme patterns (e.g., Rainbow, Christmas; 18 themes on Hampton Bay string lights) plus saveable color presets that users report cannot be deleted; an update even removed custom-color selection for fade/rainbow effects.
findings.detail: 2024-25 reviews: 'No ability to alter presets. No ability to create your own presets'; Nov 18, 2025 review complains of 'inability to delete saved color presets'; a search-surfaced review notes 'the lack of a way to save scenes'. One 2025-26 platform review (TheSmartHomie) claims 'scene creation for automations...single tap or voice command', which likely refers to Alexa/Google routines layered on top — verify in-app on 2.5.1. Guest 'choose a mood' UX therefore cannot be delivered natively by the official app: this is the single strongest pillar of the bespoke-app pitch.

findings.claim: Schedules/automations: per-device weekly time or sunrise/sunset schedules (location permission required); reviews complain there is no date option, effectively one schedule per device ('you can't have more than one schedule for any given device'), no group schedules, and no 'restore to current schedule' after power loss; vacation mode (randomized on/off) arrived in 2.1.0.
findings.detail: Users report schedule execution failures too: 'Hubspace showed the schedule was active but it would not turn [on]' and sunrise/sunset misfires attributed to the cloud scheduler. For the activation, official-app scheduling is unusable at 200-bulb scale (200 separate schedules) — scene timing must live in the bridge/kiosk.

findings.claim: Multi-user sharing is credential sharing, full stop: Home Depot's official guidance is to have family 'download the Hubspace app and then provide them your Hubspace credentials'; there are no invitations, roles, guest accounts, or per-device permissions. Multiple simultaneous sessions on one account are officially supported, and Manage Account > 'Where You're Signed In' lists active sessions.
findings.detail: Reviews confirm the friction: 'No ability to invite a guest to your account...forces you to share login information'. MFA now exists on Hubspace accounts (the HA integration documents one-time codes, and notes enabling MFA does not invalidate existing tokens) — if a staffer enables MFA on a vignette account it would break shared iPad logins mid-show, so lock MFA off on show accounts. A Dec 2025 problem report describes 'account credential rejection when attempting to share across multiple devices'.
findings.source: https://www.homedepot.com/c/ab/hubspace-faq/9ba683603be9fa5395fab9014e4790c0 (via search snippets; page 403s to bots) and https://github.com/jdeath/Hubspace-Homeassistant

findings.claim: Widgets/watch/web: iOS and Android home-screen widgets for device control arrived in v2.4 (June 9, 2026); there is no Apple Watch app (App Store listing supports iPhone, Mac with M1+, and Apple Vision Pro only) and no web app or browser control surface.
findings.detail: Mobile-only control matters for the pitch: a bespoke kiosk/tablet web UI has no official counterpart. The widgets are per-device/group shortcuts, not scene walls.

findings.claim: iPad is NOT a listed supported device: the App Store compatibility section lists iPhone (iOS 17.6+), Mac (Apple Silicon, macOS 14.6+), and Apple Vision Pro — no native iPad app, so on the four vignette iPads the official app runs as a scaled iPhone-compatibility app, and any iPad not updatable to iPadOS 17.6+ cannot run it at all.
findings.detail: This is a concrete staff-UX weakness for the activation (letterboxed phone UI at arm's length) and a clean differentiation line for a bespoke iPad-first staff app. App size 119.9 MB iOS; languages English/French/Spanish.

findings.claim: Offline behavior: Hubspace markets BLE fallback ('the only smart home solution that allows you to continue controlling your products locally with Bluetooth, in case your Wi-Fi ever goes out'), but BLE control requires the phone in radio range, responds in 'a couple of seconds' per device vs near-instant on Wi-Fi, and community integrations flatly state cloud control 'needs...the Hubspace servers'.
findings.detail: BLE fallback is per-phone, per-device, point-to-point — it cannot restore a 40-bulb zone scene quickly and is irrelevant to the kiosk bridge (cloud-only via aioafero). For the <60s recovery acceptance target, the official app's BLE path is at best a manual staff workaround for a single hero bulb, not a mitigation.

findings.claim: Top recurring pain point #1 — stale/false 'offline' states: on opening the app 'the bulb/device is listed as offline for a long time' (Nov 18, 2025, 1-star), multiple 2025 reports of 'products showing offline despite having power' and lights 'marked offline while appearing functional; manual controls unresponsive'.
findings.detail: JustUseApp's live problem mix (70 reports in 24h, fetched Sep 19, 2026): connection issues 27.0%, 'not working' 19.8%, login problems 11.7%, other 36.9%. The mechanism is visible in community code: per-device state polling with stale poll responses overwriting optimistic updates — the same cloud the kiosk bridge will use, so the kiosk UI must render optimistic state, not wait for cloud truth.

findings.claim: Top recurring pain point #2 — login/session failures: 'Hubspace logged us out and somehow one of the fan lights turned itself on'; Jan 2026 report that the app 'keeps going out' and won't permit sign-in; login problems are 11.7% of live problem reports. Under the hood, auth is Keycloak OAuth2+PKCE at accounts.hubspaceconnect.com with access tokens lasting only ~118 seconds, refreshed continuously.
findings.detail: Any refresh hiccup or Afero-side auth outage surfaces as a logout or all-devices-offline event. HowToGeek noted the platform had NO 2FA as of March 2024; MFA arrived later (now documented in community integrations). For the show: pre-login all devices, keep sessions warm, and bench an 8h soak for silent logouts.

findings.claim: Top recurring pain point #3 — command errors and reversion: users hit 'we ran into an error, please try again later' when changing colors right after opening the app, and the community integrations document a historically common quirk where 'a command seems to revert a few seconds after you set it' (stale poll overwriting the new state).
findings.detail: For a 40-bulb zone scene this manifests as a few bulbs snapping back to the old color seconds after Apply — directly threatens the 'zero wrong bulbs across 100 scene changes' acceptance target regardless of whether the official app or the bridge sends the command, since both ride the same cloud state machine. The bridge should re-assert state after ~5s as a belt-and-suspenders pass.

findings.claim: How the app behaves changing 50+ bulbs at once is UNDOCUMENTED: no public review, forum post, or article shows anyone driving 50+ Hubspace bulbs from the app; no group-size or per-account device caps are published; and whether a group action is one cloud call or N per-device calls is not publicly known.
findings.detail: Adjacent evidence points to staggered ('popcorn') behavior: the generic smart-home popcorn effect comes from per-device unicast fan-out, Afero 'rate-limits aggressively' (the HA integration floors state polling at 2s for this reason), and the aioafero library has no group/scene/room controllers at all — every community command path is per-device. The aioafero project ships MITM tooling (docs/mitm/) that can capture what the official app actually sends for a group action; running it answers the one-call-vs-N-calls question before the Sep 23 gate.

findings.claim: There is no demo mode, retail mode, guest mode, or kiosk mode in the Hubspace app — nothing in the public record (listings, FAQs, reviews, press) suggests any such feature exists. 'Party Mode' is a music-sync lighting effect on specific string-light SKUs (e.g., Hampton Bay 12-Light HB-1024SC-BK), not a demo feature.
findings.detail: Guest-facing interaction with the official app means handing over an authenticated session with full account power (delete devices, rename rooms, change Wi-Fi). Any guest-safe experience requires either heavy iPad guided-access lockdown of the official app or a bespoke front end — a core pitch point.

findings.claim: Home Depot offers NO commercial/pro Hubspace tooling: no fleet console, no property-management portal, no public API, no multi-unit dashboard. The Jan 2026 corporate announcement mentions Pros exactly once ('tailored for both everyday customers and Pros alike') with zero pro-specific features; Afero's enterprise IoT PaaS is sold to manufacturers/brands (like Home Depot), not to site operators or businesses.
findings.detail: The only quantified operational claim in Afero's Home Depot case study is device onboarding in under 60 seconds via QR scan, with Dekra/ioXT security certification. This vacuum is the commercial opening for the bespoke app pitch: 'the world's largest home improvement retailer has no operator-grade control surface for its own smart home platform.'

findings.claim: Ratings are high and stable, not degrading: iOS 4.8/5 from ~223K US ratings (≈252.5K aggregate per MWM tracker, 2.5M+ downloads), Google Play ≈4.58/5 from ~41K ratings with ~35K downloads/month; the app holds top-20 House & Home category positioning in Canada; no evidence of a post-2.0 ratings collapse.
findings.detail: The pitch should NOT claim 'the app is hated' — headline sentiment is positive, anchored on effortless QR setup and reliability for small installs. The honest framing: excellent consumer app for 5-20 devices; the complaint clusters (group schedules, scenes, sharing, offline lag) become disqualifying only at commercial/activation scale.

findings.claim: Support channel is consumer-grade and closed on one tour day: Hubspace phone support (1-877-592-5233) runs M-F 8am-7pm, Sat 9am-6pm EST — closed Sundays (tours run Oct 23-25, including Sun Oct 25), and reviews complain 'no app support...very few resources online' and 'no real way to reach out to anyone'.
findings.detail: Plan for zero vendor support during the Sunday tour window and the Oct 29 evening event (support closes 7pm EST weekdays). Escalation paths must be internal (bridge restart runbook, spare paired bulbs).

findings.claim: String-light specifics for the glow garden vignette: Hampton Bay cafe string lights (Novolink OEM) support a max of 5 daisy-chained strings per controller, ship 18 fixed preset themes, require 2.4GHz Wi-Fi, and keep running their last preset autonomously if the app/cloud disconnects.
findings.detail: The 'lights operate independently if not connected to the app with preset colors active' behavior is actually a resilience asset for the vignette: pre-stage the look, and a cloud blip won't kill it. Multiple controllers are grouped in-app for synchronized effects.

findings.claim: The bespoke app cannot replace the official app for pairing: device onboarding (QR scan, Wi-Fi provisioning) is proprietary to the official app and is its best-loved feature ('no setup wizards, no pressing and holding any buttons, no hassles'); a bespoke app rides the same account/cloud after pairing.
findings.detail: Pitch framing: bespoke = operation layer (scenes, kiosk, staff iPad control, monitoring), official app = provisioning tool used once during install week. This also bounds the bespoke product's scope honestly for the client: it is a control surface, not a full platform replacement, and it depends on an unofficial API (Afero could change auth/endpoints at any monthly release).
