bench_tests: Popcorn baseline: put 40 bulbs in one Hubspace app group on one account; tap a color change in the official app while filming the grid at 60/240fps; measure tap-to-first-bulb latency and first-to-last-bulb spread over 20 trials; repeat with the aioafero bridge issuing parallel per-device commands to the same 40 bulbs, and compare against the <2s spread target.

Group-action wire capture: use aioafero's documented MITM tooling (docs/mitm/) to capture what app 2.5.1 sends for a 40-bulb group color change — one group-object call or 40 per-device calls — and whether the cloud applies them staggered; this determines if official-app groups are even a viable fallback control path.

200-device account stress: enroll 200 bulbs on a single Hubspace account; measure app cold-start to usable home screen, time until tiles stop showing false 'offline', scroll performance, and any silent cap/throttle; then repeat with the recommended 5-account split (40 bulbs each) to validate Home Depot's separate-accounts advice.

Command-reversion watch: after each applied scene, record each 40-bulb zone for 15 seconds and count bulbs that revert to the prior state (documented 'command reverts a few seconds after you set it' quirk); verify whether a bridge-side re-assert pass at t+5s eliminates visible reverts.

8-hour concurrent-session soak: sign one vignette account into two iPads plus the kiosk bridge simultaneously (MFA off), alternate control actions every few minutes for 8h, and log forced logouts, 401s/token-refresh failures, or 'credential rejected' events; confirm expected sessions in Manage Account > Where You're Signed In.

iPad reality check: install the official app on the actual staff iPads; confirm iPadOS >= 17.6, whether it runs letterboxed in iPhone-compatibility mode, and time a staff task (change holiday living room group to a target color) — tap count and seconds — as the before/after demo for the bespoke app pitch.

Offline/recovery drill: cut venue WAN; verify the official app's Bluetooth fallback from kiosk position (per-device latency, effective range, whether a 40-bulb zone can be restored at all); restore WAN and measure time until cloud control works again versus the <60s recovery target.

MFA and preset hygiene: on a fresh show account confirm MFA can remain disabled and no forced-2FA prompts appear; then save/modify color presets on 2.5.1 and verify whether the can't-delete-preset defect still exists and whether preset clutter accumulates across grouped bulbs.
open_questions: Does an official-app group action produce ONE cloud call (group metadevice write with cloud fan-out) or N per-device calls? Nothing public answers this; MITM capture is the only way, and it sets the popcorn floor for any control path.

Is there an undocumented per-account device cap or throttling threshold near 200 devices on the Afero/Hubspace consumer tier? No limits are published; Afero support or bench loading is the only source.

Did any 2.2-2.5 release (Feb-Aug 2026) quietly add a scene/automation builder under another name? Android changelogs are generic 'Bug fixes and Improvements'; only an in-app walkthrough of 2.5.1 settles the scenes question definitively (one 2025-26 review claims 'scene creation' exists, contradicting user reviews).

Can MFA be guaranteed OFF for the life of the show accounts, and does Afero ever force-enroll MFA or expire refresh tokens on dormant/new accounts (which would break shared iPad logins and the kiosk bridge mid-show)?

What is the month-by-month ratings trajectory since the Nov 2025 2.0 redesign (needs Appfigures/Sensor Tower data or manual review pagination — headline averages look stable but redesign-era 1-star clusters are visible in Dec 2025 reviews)?
Does the app's false-'offline'-on-launch lag scale with device count (20 devices vs 200), and does it also afflict the API state the kiosk bridge reads at boot?

research.headline: A wired 12V WS2811 pixel canopy driven by xLights/xSchedule over sACN is the cheapest credible plan B (~$700-900 all-US-stock hardware, ~25ms scene latency vs the 2s target); if the canopy must remain literal A19 bulbs in E26 sockets, pre-flashed Athom WLED ESP32-C3 bulbs (~$14.63 ea, ~$3.1k for 210) drop into the same sockets and take local DDP/sACN — while flashing or locally controlling real Hubspace bulbs is a documented dead end (eFuse-locked Leedarson/ESP32 modules, cloud-only API, no Matter).

findings.claim: Ready-made C9-lookalike pixel strings cost under $1/point: Gilbert Engineering 'C9 PixaBulb' 50-node strings are 12V WS2811, 6-inch spacing, xConnect connectors, faceted white C9 covers, IP68, $38.75 per 50 ($0.78/bulb) — 200 points = 4 strings = $155 from a US (Arizona) vendor
findings.detail: These look like genuine C9 holiday bulbs (faceted cover over each node), on-theme for a late-October House Beautiful activation. 2-year warranty; vendor warns to test within 90 days and not cut strings. Cheaper raw option: HolidayCoro 100-count 12V WS2811 bullet strings $29.95/100 ($0.30/pt), in stock, ships in 24h, 0.55W/node — but bare bullets need covers (HolidayCoro's C7/C9 cover category currently lists 0 products; printable/AliExpress covers exist), so PixaBulbs are the turnkey pick.

findings.claim: Controller layer is cheap, in US stock, and hits 40fps: Falcon F16v5 $265 (in stock, 16 ports, 1024 px/port, receives 192 universes of E1.31/Art-Net/DDP); Kulp K8-PB $90-167 (8 fused ports, 800+ px/port at 40FPS, runs FPP natively); budget backups: ESPixelStick firmware (E1.31/sACN unicast+multicast and DDP, up to 680 WS2811 px) and Athom Ethernet WLED ESP32 controller $23.80
findings.detail: Any one of these drives all 200 canopy points on 1-4 ports with one $19-37 Mean Well LRS-350-12 350W PSU (200 px x 0.55W = 110W max). Advatek PixLite A4-S Mk3 (~EUR585, 1020 px/output, 24 universes Art-Net/sACN) is the pro-grade equivalent if the fabricator wants a commercial brand. At 40fps the frame period is 25ms, so a scene change visibly starts within ~1 frame + LAN transit — roughly 25-50ms, about 40-80x inside the 2s acceptance target, with first-to-last-bulb spread of one frame (all pixels update in the same frame).

findings.claim: Kiosk integration for plan B is a documented one-line HTTP call: xSchedule (xLights' player) exposes REST endpoints like /xScheduleCommand?Command=PressButton&Parameters=<label> and 'Play specified playlist <name>', plus /xScheduleQuery?Query=GetPlayingStatus and a WebSocket JSON interface with optional password
findings.detail: The existing Python kiosk bridge keeps aioafero for the 4 Hubspace vignettes and adds either (a) direct sACN/DDP sending via a Python library, or (b) HTTP calls to xSchedule playing pre-built xLights scene sequences. Scene = playlist; Apply = one GET request; status polling built in. FPP (on Kulp/Pi) offers an equivalent REST API. Zero license cost — xLights/xSchedule/FPP are free open source.

findings.claim: For a literal A19-in-socket look, Athom sells pre-flashed WLED bulbs: 12W E26/E27 color bulb on ESP32-C3 with addressable LEDs, $14.63 on sale ($19.50 list), in stock; 15W variant listed but out of stock; BR30 RGBCW $13.98 — 210 bulbs (incl. 10 spares) ≈ $3,072 and they screw into the exact same 200-socket E26 canopy grid planned for Hubspace bulbs
findings.detail: This is the like-for-like swap: identical household-bulb silhouette, same mains socket infrastructure, but locally controllable. WLED accepts E1.31/sACN, Art-Net, and DDP; docs state 170 LEDs/universe, up to 9 universes, and recommend <=510 LEDs per node for 'a fluent 25ms (40fps) or more framerate' — a whole-bulb node is trivial (a handful of LEDs). Caveats: 200 Wi-Fi clients needs 4-6 dedicated APs with unicast DDP at 10-20fps and WLED 'WiFi sleep' disabled (docs note sleep causes stutter); Athom ships from China (order by ~Sep 26 to leave buffer before Oct 20 install); WLED sync groups give a degraded-mode fallback if the sender dies.

findings.claim: Pro festoon alternatives exist at 3-13x the pixel-string price: Minleon RGB+ Triklit 42mm $129 per 20-bulb set ($6.45/bulb, 12V, 0.336W/bulb, Art-Net/sACN via NDB; one dealer shows 18 sets = 360 bulbs in stock) with NDB+16 bridge $139 (16 ports, 1600 lights, Ethernet, xLights-compatible — but sold out at that dealer); American Lighting Twinkly Pro Festoon G45 $206.95 per 20-bulb 32.8ft string ($10.35/bulb) with Controller PLUS (4 ports, 1440 LEDs, Art-Net + OSC, Ethernet+WiFi, IP65, dealer-quoted pricing)
findings.detail: Minleon 200 bulbs ≈ $1,290 + NDB $139 + PSU/cables — the classic commercial-decor route with G45-ball aesthetics and wired data (no Wi-Fi risk). Twinkly Pro 200 bulbs ≈ $2,070 + controller(s); S14 (Edison patio-bulb shape, closest to 'household bulb') exists as 'Festoon S14 PLUS' but pricing is B2B-gated (site shows EUR0,00 placeholder) — dealer quote lead time is the risk. Both accept Art-Net so latency profile matches the pixel plan.

findings.claim: Flashing real Hubspace bulbs with Tasmota/ESPHome/WLED is a proven dead end: the Home Assistant community spent 2021-2023 on a Hubspace RGBWW downlight (SKU 1005731250) containing a Leedarson/Afero LA02301 ESP32 module and found 'the bootloader has Download Mode disabled' via burned eFuses — every flash attempt failed; the only success was physically transplanting an M5Stack Stamp ESP32 and hand-wiring five GPIOs to the LED channels
findings.detail: A 200-bulb transplant is obviously not viable in 4 weeks. Current-generation Hubspace A19s are also Leedarson-built (Leedarson America is the FCC responsible party, grantee 2AB2Q; one A19 model 12CFA1960WCCT01 = FCC ID 2AB2Q-A800SG-G1Z) and Leedarson's current universal Wi-Fi/BLE module LA66701 is an ESP32-C3 SiP with embedded 4MB flash — same vendor, same lock-down posture expected (ESP32-C3 supports Secure Boot V2/flash encryption and Afero's whole platform pitch is hardware security). Treat custom firmware on Hubspace hardware as OFF the table for this show.

findings.claim: There is no local-network API for Hubspace and no usable BLE control path for lights: every community integration (jdeath/Hubspace-Homeassistant + aioafero, homebridge-hubspace, hubspace-ng) talks to the Afero cloud; the only BLE work (jdeath/hubspace_ble) targets Defiant locks, is explicitly 'a future Home Assistant Integration', and its test script 'only extracts the device ID and some other unknown data at this time'
findings.detail: The 'HubSpaceLocal' repo that sounds promising (DaedalusStudios/HubSpaceLocal, 'direct connection') is just a fork of Home Assistant core with no evident working local protocol — not a real path. Additionally the LA66701 module manual states Wi-Fi and BLE 'cannot transmit simultaneously', which explains why a bulb already joined to Wi-Fi is not a reliable BLE control target even in principle. Conclusion: actual Hubspace bulbs can only be driven through the Afero cloud (aioafero), so plan B must swap hardware, not protocols.

findings.claim: No Hubspace A19 has Matter support and none is announced for late 2026: HowToGeek (Mar 2024) reported no native Matter or HomeKit; the Dec 16 2025 GearBrain 'Hubspace 2.0' deep-dive lists only Alexa and Google Assistant as ecosystem layers with no Matter/HomeKit/local-control mention; Home Depot's own Jan 7 2026 'Whole Home Integration Powered by Hubspace' corporate post touts Hubspace 2.0 Connect, 200+ products, Kwikset locks (2026) and Texas Instruments chips — and never says the word Matter
findings.detail: So a 'wait for Matter and control the same bulbs locally' plan B does not exist for this October. (Some SEO-grade sites like smarthomiehub.com claim 'Matter-enabled Hubspace products integrate with Apple Home' but this contradicts every primary/dated source and should be disregarded.) Even if a Matter bulb SKU appeared, 200-node Matter-over-WiFi group scene latency would itself need a bench pass — moot for this timeline.

findings.claim: The hybrid pattern used in real retail is 'real product where hands touch it, dedicated show control where the spectacle is': Philips Hue's Best Buy endcap was a purpose-built 8-ft interactive fixture by display fabricator LG&P demonstrating dimming/brightening/color on a controlled rig, and brand-activation pixel work is normally driven by show-control tools like ENTTEC ELM outputting DMX/Art-Net/sACN/KiNET live or on a timeline — not by the consumer cloud app path
findings.detail: Recommended hybrid for Charleston: keep genuine Hubspace hardware in the 4 staff-paced vignettes (low device count, staff can pace the demo, cloud latency tolerable) plus a touchable 'hero shelf' of real EcoSmart A19s at eye level near the kiosk; run the 200-point canopy on pixels/WLED via sACN where latency and zero-wrong-bulb targets actually bite. Latency-hiding UX if any cloud path stays guest-facing: optimistic UI — reflect the chosen mood on the kiosk screen within 100ms (humans notice delay at ~100ms), play a branded 'mixing your color' preview animation sized to cover worst-case cloud propagation, and stage the physical reveal (e.g., zone-by-zone sweep) so the first visible change is a pre-armed fast command and stragglers land inside the choreography; roll back UI on failure.

findings.claim: RECOMMENDATION — cheapest credible plan B, orderable this week, install-ready by mid-Oct: 'C9 pixel canopy' ≈ $700-900: 5x Gilbert C9 PixaBulb 50-node strings $194 (200 pts + 50 spares), Falcon F16v5 $265 (plus a $24-35 ESPixelStick/Athom-Ethernet cold spare), 2x Mean Well LRS-350-12 ~$75, xConnect extensions/tees/fusing/mounting ~$150; xLights/xSchedule free; kiosk fires xSchedule REST or raw sACN from Python
findings.detail: Every acceptance target passes with huge margin: scene start ~25-50ms (target <2s), full scene correct in 1 frame (target <5s), first-to-last spread ~1 frame (target <2s), zero cloud dependency so 'recovery after internet returns' is vacuous (controller + player run on show LAN), 8h soak limited only by PSU thermals. Trade-off: bulbs read as C9/festoon decor, not A19 household bulbs. If creative insists on A19-in-socket realism, upgrade path is the Athom WLED swap (~$3.1k, order by ~Sep 26, bench Wi-Fi density first) reusing the identical E26 socket grid; mid option is Minleon Triklit (~$1.5k, wired, G45 ball look). Decision rule for the Sep 23 gate: if Hubspace cloud misses targets on the bench, green-light PixaBulb order same day (in-stock, days to ship) and keep Hubspace hardware in vignettes so the activation still demos real product.

Soak: run xSchedule looping 40fps sequences on 200 pixels for 8h; log controller frame drops (FPP/Falcon status page), PSU and controller temperature at the 4h/8h marks, and run a scripted 100-scene-change pass photographing the grid after each change to prove zero wrong/missed bulbs.

Athom WLED A19 passability + Wi-Fi density: order 10-20 bulbs NOW (China lead time); (a) side-by-side lit comparison against an EcoSmart Hubspace A19 behind the canopy diffusion — does it read as the same household bulb to a guest at 8ft? (b) join all bulbs to one dedicated 2.4GHz AP, drive with unicast DDP at 10 and 20fps, measure apply-to-light latency and packet loss over 2h, then extrapolate AP count for 200 nodes (target <=50 clients/AP); (c) disable WiFi sleep per WLED docs and re-measure; (d) kill the DDP sender and verify WLED preset/sync-group fallback keeps a static scene.

Offline/recovery: with plan-B rig on an isolated show LAN (no internet), verify scenes still trigger (should be identical — no cloud dependency); cut mains to controller+PSU mid-scene, restore, and time to autoresume playlist (FPP/xSchedule autostart) — accept <60s.

Rigging/electrical fit: confirm PixaBulb string weight and 6-inch spacing maps onto the 20x10 grid geometry (10x20ft = 24-inch pitch, so pixels need re-spacing into sockets/clips or a 2-ft-pitch custom-spaced order — Gilbert/HolidayCoro sell custom spacing); for the Athom path confirm 200 E26 socket circuit load with bulbs capped at a preset brightness (200x12W worst case = 2.4kW; measure real draw at show brightness).

contradictions: Conclave maturity and dating: the performance researcher dates the push channel to June 2026 (PR #77 merged 2026-06-08, '8.0.0 in June') while aioafero-source and ha-integration date the shipped feature to v9.3.0 on Sep 15 2026 ('4 days old'; 8.0.0 on Aug 6 per PyPI). The PyPI-dated side is stronger (verifiable release history, cited twice); at best the code sat ~3 months in a branch with 4 days of production exposure — so afero-platform's headline claim that Conclave 'gives you sub-2s state feedback' rests on an essentially just-released component.

Conclave latency: afero-platform's headline asserts sub-2s state feedback; performance states no push-latency measurement exists anywhere ('nobody has published tap-to-push-event latency'). Performance is right — the sub-2s figure is an assumption, and it matters doubly because Conclave is also the proposed verification rail: an unmeasured feedback channel is being used to certify an unmeasured control channel.

Throttle failure signature: ha-integration claims 'the 429-retry code proves Afero does send 429s'; afero-platform infers 403s (the Aug 2026 403-pause feature exists because users hit them); performance's only real-world datapoint is silent payload degradation (device names vanishing at 10s polling) with no 429 at all. The 429 claim is weakest — defensive client code proves nothing. The 403-pause feature and observed silent degradation are actually evidenced, and silent degradation is the most dangerous form because it defeats retry logic and optimistic caches; the bridge must validate response shapes, not just status codes.

The load-bearing '2-second polling floor': four sections cite it as the 'community-established/observed' rate limit, but the sources are (a) a config-validation floor in the jdeath HA UI and (b) one README sentence from Emkraan — a zero-star integration created Jul 2026 with no community validation — while jdeath itself (381 stars) defaulted to 30s then 900s. The floor is folklore, not measurement, and nothing public constrains burst WRITE behavior at all, which is the operation the show actually needs.

Server-side scene/group primitive: app-reverse-eng elevates the decompiled 'AferoClientSceneMixin' to proof that scenes are first-class API entities in the shipping app, but app-ux documents that the shipping app has NO user-composable scene feature at all (only per-device/group presets), and aioafero-source/ha-integration confirm no community code has ever observed a group/scene write. App-ux's evidence is stronger: a mixin name in a generic Afero SDK is fully consistent with dead/vestigial code. Consequence: the decisive MITM capture must target a GROUP action (groups do exist in the app UI); one-call fan-out should be priced as unlikely-but-cheap-to-check, not a probable rescue.

Wire-level facts disagree: afero-platform and app-reverse-eng (quoting code) say state calls open TLS to api2.afero.net with a Host: semantics2.afero.net header override; aioafero-source says device traffic goes 'on semantics2.afero.net'; performance's dig shows the two hostnames resolve to different IPs, so the distinction is real for throttle keying and the /v1-to-/v2 probe. The code-verbatim side is stronger. Related transcription conflict: aioafero-source quotes room/home typeIds as 'metadata.room'/'metadata.home' while app-reverse-eng's test-dump quote says 'metadevice.home/room' — one is mis-transcribed, discovery filters depend on exact strings, and it is desk-checkable in an hour before any bench code is written.

What a 2xx PUT means: ha-integration suggests Apply-confirmation 'can come from PUT responses'; app-reverse-eng and afero-platform cite official Afero docs that attribute writes are asynchronous ('the API call may return before the actual write takes place') and note aioafero updates its cache optimistically from the PUT response. The official-docs side wins: HTTP success is cloud acceptance, not bulb application, so acceptance measurement and the show-ops dashboard must be built on Conclave echo and/or camera, never on PUT status.

BLE as fallback: hardware calls app BLE control 'the on-site emergency lever if the venue uplink dies'; app-ux shows it is per-phone, per-device, seconds-per-command; plan-b cites the Leedarson module manual stating Wi-Fi and BLE cannot transmit simultaneously, making BLE control of a Wi-Fi-associated bulb doubtful in principle. The skeptical side is stronger — treat BLE as a single-hero-bulb parlor trick and dual-WAN (Peplink) as the only real uplink mitigation.

Account sharding as a throughput multiplier: ha-integration treats the troubleshooting doc's 'clients compete for the same quota' as validating that 5 accounts multiply write budget; performance counters that there is zero public proof of aggregate scaling and per-IP throttling is unknown (all five accounts NAT through one venue IP). Performance is right — the multiplier is a hypothesis resting on one sentence, cheaply falsifiable at the bench by running two accounts through one IP simultaneously.

Current A19 silicon: hardware pins the exact hero SKU to ESP32-U4WD via its own FCC grant (SKU-specific, strongest); plan-b says Leedarson's 'current universal module' LA66701 is an ESP32-C3; network-scale still hedges 'ESP32-class or Realtek'. Hardware wins for the planned 12-series bulb; the C3 likely belongs to newer/other SKUs and the Realtek hedge is dead. Residual consequence is only Wi-Fi behavior nuance (power-save, min-rate tolerance) — a bench item regardless.

Sub-60s recovery with stock components: aioafero-source reads the poll-loop backoff as compatible with the target ('first retry ~30s'); ha-integration/Emkraan document that the stock loop historically swallowed exceptions and froze on stale data indefinitely, and that 500/502/connection errors are not retried at all — and the one documented Afero outage (Jul 27 2026) was exactly 500s+timeouts. The pessimistic side is stronger for shipped code: recovery must come from a bridge-owned watchdog proven with WAN-cut drills, and whether 9.3.0 fixed the silent-stale loop is unverified.

How proven the stack is at scale: afero-platform calls the path 'technically stable (two active HA integrations do this at scale)' while ha-integration documents the largest known deployment at 143 devices — with never-root-caused bootstrap failures — and typical installs of 1-7 devices. ha-integration is correct: 200 bulbs is beyond all recorded field experience and should be framed to the client as original research, not proven practice.

Latency baseline optimism: the only end-to-end command datapoint is '1-2s when healthy' from a 2023 issue on the obsolete architecture, yet several sections treat 95%-under-2s as plausible. If the modern cloud-to-bulb visible floor is anywhere near 1s, the whole 2s budget is consumed by one bulb before any fan-out queueing. Neither side has current data — this is unresolvable from sources and is the second thing the bench must measure.
bench_priorities: 1. Write-burst envelope and throttle signature (the go/no-go number): on one account, ladder concurrent state PUTs (5, 10, 20, 40 in flight, then sustained repeats) and record where and HOW Afero pushes back — 429 with/without Retry-After, hard 403, connection resets, or silent response degradation / dropped or merged writes — plus PUT RTT distribution; then repeat with two accounts simultaneously behind one NAT IP to separate per-account from per-IP keying. This single experiment decides whether 40-PUT zone waves fit inside 2s and whether the 5-account shard multiplies budget at all.

2. True bulb-side latency and spread at one full zone (minimum 40 bulbs): measure Apply-to-first-visible-change and first-to-last spread with camera-timestamped video over 100+ scene cycles (p50/p95), logging Conclave attr_change arrival alongside to calibrate whether Conclave echo can stand in for photons; establish the single-bulb visible floor (300ms vs 1.5s decides whether the 2s target is in play) and per-bulb variance from Wi-Fi power save.

3. MITM the official app performing a 40-bulb GROUP action and preset apply (aioafero ships the mitmproxy how-to): one server-side call or N per-device calls? Simultaneously probe the legacy rules engine (POST /v1/accounts/{id}/rules + execute_actions) and /v2 semantics paths with a hubspace_android token, and dump raw metadevices expansions looking for group/scene typeIds. One afternoon that could collapse 200 PUTs into 5.

4. Conclave 9.3.0 under load and across failure: 8h soak at maximum assembled device count with repeated scene bursts (does the serial-lock event processor back up and delay confirmations?), conclaveAccess token re-mint over multi-hour uptime, then deliberate WAN cuts timing detection-to-full-resync against the <60s target — confirming the historic silent-stale-freeze mode is gone or watchdogged.

5. Auth and session realism: read the actual Keycloak expires_in (118s is only a fallback constant); run 5 accounts refreshing for 8h; log in from a fresh IP/device to characterize OTP challenges and lockout thresholds; verify pre-minted refresh tokens survive an IP move (the venue scenario); confirm MFA stays off; and run the official app concurrently with the bridge on one account to observe quota competition and stale-poll state reversion.

6. Provisioning and fleet mechanics at cadence: claim 40 bulbs rapidly on one account (does anti-abuse bite? can two phones claim concurrently?); QR cross-account transfer semantics (are Wi-Fi credentials preserved? does it work while the bulb is online?); actual restore-values behavior after a power cut; factory-reset sequence on the production SKU; a live 12-series A19 device dump (effect list, CCT shape vs the A21 assumptions); firmware census, force-update-then-freeze, and whether OTA can be deferred.

7. RF and power-restore behavior on the planned network: 802.11b-rates-disabled join test and WPA2-only join on the exact SKU; the SSID architecture decision (single SSID vs 5 zone-pinned SSIDs) validated under a full-scene cascade with channel-utilization capture; 40-bulb circuit power-restore thundering herd (association+DHCP+TLS storm) and staggered bring-up timing.

8. Kill-switch and plan-B trigger drill: simulate 403-everything and total WAN loss mid-'show' to time detection, operator messaging, and recovery; rehearse the same-day PixaBulb order package — and force the creative A19-look-vs-C9-look decision now, because the Athom WLED order cutoff (~Sep 26) lands three days after the gate.
missing_angles: The gate itself is undesigned: no researcher states how many bulbs the Sep 23 bench will actually have or what numeric pass/fail thresholds apply. A bench can prove failure at any scale but can only prove PASS with at least one full 40-bulb zone plus explicit headroom math (e.g., zone applies in <1s at concurrency X with zero throttle events across N cycles, therefore 5 parallel accounts inferred safe). Pass criteria must be agreed before Sep 23 or the gate outputs a shrug.

Verification instrumentation is unscoped: 'zero wrong bulbs across 100 scene changes' is ~20,000 bulb-state verifications, and Conclave alone cannot ground-truth them (it reports cloud state, not photons — a hung bulb can still echo). Nobody has scoped the camera/CV rig or Conclave-ledger tooling needed both to score acceptance and to detect wrong bulbs live during show operations.

The acceptance criteria contradict the physics of the chosen path: an eventually-consistent cloud with async acks and no delivery guarantee cannot promise literal zero misses. The bridge needs a read-back/re-assert reconciliation loop, whose added write volume itself interacts with the unknown throttle (nobody analyzed this feedback loop), and the client-facing target should be renegotiated to 'wrong bulbs self-heal within N seconds' before it becomes a failed test on paper.

Cross-zone scene coherence: one guest 'mood' equals 5 parallel zone applies across 5 accounts/bridge instances; a single throttled zone yields a visibly mismatched canopy. No design exists for cross-zone commit choreography, partial-failure retry ordering, or what the kiosk displays while one zone lags.

Diurnal cloud load: a consumer IoT cloud peaks on weekday evenings — exactly the Oct 29 evening event window — yet no soak or latency plan samples time-of-day variance. Bench bursts should run morning and evening, and the 8h soak should span a real evening peak.

Same-account interference policy: staff will have the official app open against the same accounts the bridge drives; the app is another writer and poller that competes for quota and can revert bridge state (the documented stale-poll overwrite). No operational rule exists for when staff may touch the app during show hours.

Spares and swap logistics: no plan for pre-claimed, zone-assigned, firmware-matched spare bulbs (a mid-show swap should be a socket swap, not a 5-minute app ceremony), no failure-rate expectation for a 9-day powered install, and no custody plan for 200 QR cards that function as literal ownership tokens (scanning one transfers the device).

Bench-vs-show hardware consistency and procurement: the bench needs a meaningful bulb count within 4 days and the show needs 200+ of one SKU by mid-Oct; nothing covers store stock and lead time, batch/firmware heterogeneity between bench units and show units, or that partner-controlled OTA can change firmware after benching anyway.

The THD authorization letter and Afero heads-up channel have no owner or deadline: risk-legal defined the artifact but no one is tasked to obtain it this week, even though it is simultaneously the cheapest legal de-risk for the show, the only plausible early-warning channel for late-October backend changes (Hubspace 2.0 rollout train), and the gating precondition for the upsell pitch.
upsell_risks: Counterparty conflict is structural: the 'better app' pitch asks Home Depot to bless replacing software authored by Afero (the Play package is literally io.afero.partner.hubspace) — the same vendor whose cooperation any licensed path requires, and who has ignored community partnership requests since at least Oct 2025. A realistic outcome is THD/Afero simply internalizing the idea; Hubspace 2.0's monthly release cadence shows an active roadmap next to which an agency app is easy to absorb.

Platform kill-switch and silent drift: the product rides hubspace_android impersonation that Afero can fingerprint (TLS, UA, cadence) and 403 at will; the Myko migration proves a partner-side backend change kills all community access overnight with zero notice; the official app is already on /v2 endpoints while the community sits on /v1; no contract, no deprecation policy, no status page. A client-facing SLA cannot honestly be written on this substrate.

Legal posture flips when commercialized: the activation itself is defensible (owned devices, THD sanction obtainable, Van Buren/Chamberlain-friendly), but a distributed commercial client plainly breaches the personal-noncommercial ToU, faces App Review rejection risk for unauthorized third-party service use, and — if a sanctioned Service Agreement is ever signed — inherits Afero's paper terms: usage monitoring, instant revocation, 30-day data retention, and a no-publicity clause constraining even the case study.

Maintenance economics are open-ended: auth is HTML-scraped Keycloak that breaks on any login-flow or theme change, the platform ships roughly monthly, and the community library cut three breaking majors in eight months. A fixed-price deliverable silently becomes a perpetual reverse-engineering retainer; no cost model for that has been sketched.

It can never truly be a 'replacement': BLE provisioning is proprietary and unreverse-engineered (softhub session crypto unsolved), so the bespoke app is a control/experience layer that still depends on the official app for onboarding. Pitching 'replacement' overpromises and invites scope dispute; the honest scope is operator/kiosk/fleet layer.

The pitch narrative must invert: the official app holds 4.8/5 from ~223k ratings, so 'your app is bad' fails on contact. The evidence-backed wedge is the total absence of any commercial/kiosk/fleet/operator tooling for Hubspace — and that wedge is strongest pitched WITH THD/Afero as a licensed white-label build, which converts the platform-risk liability into the product's moat.

The activation is the demo: if Afero blocks the bridge or a visible failure occurs mid-show, the upsell dies with it; if it succeeds, the show telemetry (uptime, scene counts, latency percentiles) is the pitch collateral — but capturing and publishing that needs case-study/brand permission not yet in the SOW, and any later tightening of OTP, MFA, or anti-bot posture could make the demo unreproducible by pitch time.
gaps.verdict: Plausible but wholly unproven at this scale: the only architecture with a real chance is 5 accounts x 40 bulbs driven by a custom bridge (patched connection limits, bounded 10-25-in-flight fan-out per account, Conclave-or-camera confirmation, and a reconcile/re-assert loop), because stock aioafero — 3 connections, ~0.75s total retry budget, optimistic cache — fails the targets by construction. Whether that shape passes hangs on two numbers that exist nowhere in public: Afero's per-account/per-IP write-burst tolerance and the modern cloud-to-bulb visible-latency floor (the only datapoint, 1-2s from 2023, would consume the entire budget on its own). The single biggest threat is the unquantified write throttle striking in its nastiest observed form — silent response degradation rather than clean 429s — mid-show, on a cloud with no status page, no Sunday support, and no contractual recourse. A secondary structural problem: 'zero wrong bulbs across 100 changes' is unattainable as literally written on an async eventually-consistent cloud and must be renegotiated to self-healing semantics before it becomes a paper failure. Given plan B (PixaBulb/sACN, in stock, ~$700-900) beats every target by 40-80x, the rational posture is: bench items 1-3 decide the canopy, Hubspace hardware stays in the vignettes regardless, and the creative C9-vs-A19 decision plus the THD authorization letter get forced this week, not after the gate.
